papers.title: ProTracer: Proprioception-Guided Failure Diagnosis in Robot Manipulation
papers.summary: This paper presents a comprehensive framework for robot manipulation failure analysis that includes binary failure detection, failure categorization, explanation generation, and the additional capability of failure onset localization, which aims to identify the earliest moment at which a robot execution deviates from a valid task-completion trajectory and is ultimately followed by task failure. To address these tasks, we propose ProTracer, a training-free framework that leverages existing Vision-Language Models (VLMs) together with proprioceptive signals for failure analysis. Our method uses proprioceptive dynamics to identify temporally informative action boundaries and converts richer robot-state signals into structured natural-language descriptions that can be jointly analyzed together with visual observations by the VLM. This design combines the temporal precision of proprioceptive signals with the multimodal reasoning capabilities of modern VLMs without requiring additional model training. We further introduce FailTime, a benchmark with synchronized visual and proprioceptive observations for evaluating conventional failure diagnosis tasks as well as failure onset localization. Experiments demonstrate that ProTracer achieves strong performance across both conventional failure diagnosis tasks and the newly introduced failure onset localization task, highlighting the importance of proprioceptive reasoning for fine-grained temporal failure analysis.

papers.title: FlatClip: Reusing Image Foundation Models for fMRI Representation Learning via Cortical Flatmaps
papers.summary: Can the spatial organization of cortical activity help transfer frozen image representations to fMRI prediction? We introduce FlatClip, which renders cortical activity as anatomy-linked flatmaps and extracts features with a frozen SigLIP2 encoder. Only a lightweight downstream probe is trained, without fMRI-specific encoder pretraining or fine-tuning. Across four resting-state benchmarks, FlatClip outperforms the evaluated ROI-level baselines on HCP and ADNI, but is weaker on PPMI and below the strongest voxel-level models overall. On NSD visual-fMRI decoding, restricting inputs to visual or NSD-provided task-active cortex improves recognition over whole-cortex inputs. Spatial perturbations reduce performance with both retrained and fixed readouts, and anatomy-linked arrangements outperform cortical-pixel permutations across three colormaps. Together, these results demonstrate a practical route for reusing image-pretrained features in fMRI and highlight cortical arrangement and input-region selection as important design choices. Code is available at https://github.com/OneMore1/FlatClip.

papers.title: MorphoBranch: A Fine-Structure-Preserving Workbench for Morphometric Analysis of Branched Cellular Structures
papers.summary: Background and Objectives: Fluorescence-labeled cellular arbors provide readouts of neuronal and microglial morphology, but fine and weakly labeled processes are prone to fragmentation and false connections that bias skeleton-based measurements. We present MorphoBranch, a fine-structure-preserving, human-reviewable workbench for morphometry of branched cellular structures. Methods: MorphoBranch combines a deterministic Morphometry Engine with an LLM-assisted Refinement Engine. The Mor- phometry Engine implements an image-to-graph workflow integrating multiscale structural evidence extraction, hysteresis segmen- tation, evidence-constrained skeleton refinement, and graph-based morphometry. The Refinement Engine maps natural-language requests to registered actions for parameter adjustment, preview execution, metric reporting, and unsupported-request handling, while image processing and quantitative computation remain deterministic and reviewable. Results: MorphoBranch was evaluated on two public neuronal axon datasets, AxonMIP and AxonStack, and the in-house Cell- Morph dataset of microglial fluorescence images. It achieved the highest Skeleton F1 and clDice and the lowest length-estimation error among the evaluated methods on all three datasets, while also achieving the highest Dice and IoU on AxonMIP and Axon- Stack. Across 150 natural-language tasks, the Refinement Engine achieved a 94.0% end-to-end success rate. Conclusions: These results demonstrate that MorphoBranch provides a reproducible, human-reviewable workflow for mor- phometric analysis of branched cellular structures. It supports fine-structure-preserving quantification across neuronal axon and microglial fluorescence images while maintaining inspectable and reproducible analysis workflows.

papers.title: LoopWAM: Closed-Loop Generalist Policy Improvement from Deployment Rollouts
papers.summary: Scaling expert demonstrations alone does not enable generalist robot policies to improve from deployment. Real-world rollouts contain successes, suboptimal behavior, and failures: imitating every recorded action can reinforce poor behavior, while filtering out failures discards evidence of physical interactions and their consequences. We introduce LoopWAM, a closed-loop world-action model that learns directly from this full quality spectrum, using rollouts from both itself and other deployed policies. Source-dependent noise sampling unifies behavior learning and action-conditioned world modeling, while quality steering and quality-weighted supervision retain full video supervision across qualities and regulate action imitation. Video and action tokens interact throughout parallel denoising, allowing learned consequences to inform action generation directly. On RoboChallenge Table30-V2, three deployment-and-training rounds raise success from 23.67% to 43.33%, a 19.7-percentage-point gain, with a final score of 56.80. LoopWAM also achieves 94.5% average success on RoboTwin 2.0 and 49.5% overall success on RoboCasa365 without additional embodied pretraining, obtaining the best overall results among the compared methods across all three benchmarks. On challenging shirt folding task, two rounds of deployment-driven improvement after single-task post-training raise success from 13.20% to 55.56%. These results demonstrate closed-loop improvement from mixed-quality experience under both multi-task learning and single-task post-training. Project page: https://loop-wam.github.io/

papers.title: AeroProp-X: An Open-Source, Self-Verifying Method-of-Characteristics Toolkit for Edge-Capable Rocket Nozzle Design and Aerothermodynamic Analysis
papers.summary: The design of supersonic rocket nozzles by the Method of Characteristics is a mature discipline, yet the software that implements it is frequently either proprietary, heavyweight, or opaque, which limits reproducibility and classroom and field use. This paper presents AeroProp-X, an open-source, dependency-light toolkit that synthesizes shock-free minimum-length nozzle contours and evaluates their ideal aerothermodynamic performance entirely on commodity hardware without graphics acceleration or network access. The central contribution is methodological rather than physical: the planar characteristics solver is made self-verifying by exploiting an exact gas-dynamic invariant, namely that the computed exit wall height ratio must equal the isentropic area ratio at the design Mach number, so that every generated contour reports its own discretization error automatically. We describe the governing theory, the layered software architecture, and the synthesis algorithm, and we validate the implementation against analytic compressible-flow tables and against the expansion ratios of historical flight engines. The solver reproduces tabulated gas-dynamic quantities to table precision and converges to the exact area ratio with relative error below three parts in ten thousand, while remaining small enough to run interactively on an embedded-class processor. We argue that built-in verifiability, dependency minimalism, and explicit scoping of the ideal-flow assumptions together make the tool well suited to education, preliminary design, and reproducible research.

papers.title: Physics-informed Kolmogorov-Arnold networks (PIKANs) for noise-robust reconstruction of boiling heat flux from infrared measurements
papers.summary: Recovering a noise-amplified inverse quantity from corrupted boundary data is a recurring problem in physics-informed learning for real-world applications. Specifically, small perturbations in the measured field are magnified through the spatial derivatives needed to reconstruct the target, and hence conventional discretization solvers turn them into large unphysical oscillations. We study this problem through the reconstruction of local time-resolved nucleate-boiling heat flux, which cannot be measured directly and must be inferred from infrared surface temperatures by solving an unsteady three-dimensional heat-conduction problem with sharp and rapidly evolving liquid-vapor interface gradients. We show that neither network architecture nor optimizer alone overcomes the spectral bias that smooths away these interface-scale features, and that the two must be addressed jointly. Our approach combines a Chebyshev physics-informed Kolmogorov-Arnold network (PIKAN) backbone, a quasi-second-order (SOAP) optimizer, and a temperature-annealed residual-based resampling scheme that concentrates collocation points at high-residual interface regions. Trained directly on experimental infrared measurements imposed as a boundary condition, the network resolves high-frequency bubble signatures and the high-flux distribution tail much better than a Fourier-feature PINN of equal size and training budget. In particular, it selectively filters measurement noise while preserving the physically meaningful high-frequency features, suppressing the spurious oscillations that contaminate finite-volume reconstructions and yielding more physically consistent heat-flux estimates from noisy experimental data.

papers.title: Representation-split Carleman lattice Boltzmann with near-unit step success probability on quantum computers
papers.summary: The Carleman lattice Boltzmann method replaces the quadratic collision of the lattice Boltzmann equation by a linear map on a lifted state. Existing block encodings of this map succeed with probability $10^{-5}$ to $10^{-2}$ per step, so that the probability of a multi-step evolution decays exponentially with the number of steps. This study develops multi-relaxation-time Carleman lattice Boltzmann, a representation split in which the Carleman-lifted collision is performed in a moment basis on the amplitude-encoded state, while streaming remains a permutation in population space. The level-2 hierarchy closes under collision but not under streaming, which generates the work of pressure, advection and stress on the momentum flux. The state therefore remains the full pair array, and the moment representation is an orthogonal change of basis of the population one, with identical dynamics and truncation error. The operator to be block encoded changes with the basis, and with it the success probability of a quantum step. In the weighted Hermite basis with the amplitude encoding $f_i/\sqrt{w_i}$, the relaxation is a diagonal operator of norm one, and the level-2 collision stage becomes this diagonal plus a sparse coupling from products of conserved moments. A structured block encoding of this form raises the single-step success probability on the D2Q9 lattice from $10^{-2}$ for the best population encoding to 0.98. With the pair sector in relative coordinates and scaled, one step requires $O(\log^2 N)$ Toffoli gates and is verified by statevector simulation. The encoding and readout overhead of a $T$-step run is then polynomial in $T$ and $N$ rather than accumulating a factor $p^T$. For resolved flows, the remaining exponential loss in coherent multi-step Carleman lattice Boltzmann evolution is set by the non-equilibrium norm relaxed by dissipation rather than by the block encoding.

papers.title: On the Assessment of Domain Decomposition Approaches in Extended Physics-Informed Neural Networks for the Shock-Dominated Burgers Equation
papers.summary: Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs) provide a mesh-free framework for solving partial differential equations but often struggle with sharp gradients and shock-dominated solutions. Extended Physics-Informed Neural Networks (XPINNs) address this challenge through domain decomposition; however, the effects of decomposition design, overlap, and local network capacity on solution accuracy remain insufficiently characterized. This work presents a systematic assessment of domain decomposition configurations for XPINNs applied to the one-dimensional viscous Burgers equation ($\nu=0.01/\pi$). We compare a standard PINN, a conventional XPINN, a shock-focused XPINN with increased network capacity in the shock-containing subdomain, and overlapping XPINNs with different overlap widths. All configurations are trained using a common protocol based on Adam, L-BFGS refinement, and ten Residual-based Adaptive Refinement (RAR) cycles. Performance is evaluated against a reference solution using global and shock-region relative $L_2$ and $L_\infty$ errors, maximum PDE residuals, and interface continuity errors. The results show that decomposition design strongly affects XPINN accuracy and shock resolution. Among the overlapping configurations, the smallest overlap provides the best accuracy, while larger overlaps degrade performance. The shock-focused XPINN achieves the lowest overall solution errors, indicating that increased local network capacity can provide greater benefit than increasing overlap alone. RAR produces the largest improvements during early refinement stages, followed by increasingly non-monotonic changes in accuracy. These findings highlight the importance of jointly considering decomposition, interface coupling, network capacity, and adaptive refinement for shock-dominated problems.

papers.title: Second-Order Homogenization of Particulate Elastomeric Composites for Structural-Scale Damage Analysis
papers.summary: Damage prediction in particulate elastomeric composites is challenging due to the strong material heterogeneity, nearly incompressible behavior of the matrix, and the presence of localized stress concentrations arising from matrix-inclusion interactions. In the present work, a computational framework is developed for damage propagation analysis of particulate elastomeric composite structures. The effective constitutive response of the heterogeneous material is first determined using the second-order homogenization method. The resulting homogenized response is subsequently used to identify equivalent hyperelastic material parameters for structural simulations. A three-parameter isotropic damage model is incorporated to capture damage-induced softening. A mixed displacement-pressure finite element formulation, is used to alleviate volumetric locking associated with nearly incompressible property of elastomers. The proposed framework is validated through full-scale simulations and homogenized response involving composites with varying inclusion volume fractions. Numerical investigations demonstrate that the homogenized models is able to reproduce the global force-displacement response within 2% error and damage evolution characteristics of the heterogeneous composites while significantly reducing the computational cost.

papers.title: Energy-Stable Parametric Operator Inference across Regime Transitions: Application to Unconfined Buoyant Plumes in Stratified Ambients
papers.summary: Buoyant plumes in stratified ambients arise in wildfire smoke transport, ventilation, and pollutant dispersion, where many-query prediction requires models that stay accurate and stable as the dynamics transition from free rise to internal-wave trapping. Operator Inference (OpInf) learns polynomial reduced models from snapshots, and the Boussinesq plume depends affinely on the squared buoyancy frequency $N^2$. However, this compatibility masks two stability gaps: a single affine operator family can distort the per-parameter dynamics into unstable spectra, and for quadratic OpInf models, finite-time blowup is governed by a cubic energy injection channel from the inferred quadratic operator. To address these gaps, we develop cyclic-skew regime-bridged OpInf (CR-OpInf). We derive an affine-inadequacy diagnostic that links the departure from a shared affine family to destabilizing spectral drift before integration. In place of the shared affine fit, we interpolate per-parameter operators with a Gaussian kernel. We also extend the cyclic-skew quadratic constraint to the buoyancy-source-forced parametric setting, closing the cubic energy channel and isolating this closure as the boundedness mechanism. We further introduce a regime-bridging basis split that resolves free rise and trapped intrusion structures while preserving the cyclic-skew structure under convex interpolation. Applied to an unconfined Boussinesq plume and a viscous Burgers problem spanning a smooth-to-shock transition, CR-OpInf remains bounded for five training horizons, avoids the divergence of affine and unconstrained variants, tracks the plume rise, and recovers stratification-dependent rise scaling at moderate horizons. To our knowledge, this is the first parametric OpInf study of an unconfined stratified plume.

papers.title: BBun: an unsteady vortex-ring panel method for interacting lifting bodies, box wings and propellers
papers.summary: This report documents BBun (Blunt Body unsteady), a low-order code for the unsteady potential flow around one or more interacting three-dimensional bodies. The bodies are represented by vortex rings (piecewise-constant doublets) with a Neumann boundary condition; free vortex sheets are shed from the trailing edges and, optionally, from the tips, and convected in time, with an implicit unsteady Kutta condition. The report describes the choices that make the discretization consistent and convergent (a single desingularized kernel per wake line, a bordered factorization of the singular Neumann problem, interior velocity conditions for the nearly singular mode of ring-shaped bodies, the detection of the separation lines from the grid connectivity) and the extensions to several bodies, box wings, symmetric configurations (image method), non-lifting bodies, rigidly rotating bodies (propellers), the unsteady Bernoulli equation, a wake-body collision treatment and a strip-wise integral boundary layer. The verification and validation are reported in full: potential flow around a sphere, sensitivity and grid convergence, the two-dimensional limit, an independent vortex-lattice method, the NACA 0015 wing of McAlister and Takahashi (loads and chordwise pressures), the NACA 0012 profile drag, the biplane of Knight and Noyes, Prandtl's best wing system, Wagner's function and blade-element momentum theory for a propeller. A complete aircraft with counter-rotating tractor propellers illustrates the use of the code.

papers.title: Thermochemically Constrained Multiscale Laplace Neural Operator to Learn Stiff Chemical Kinetics with Conditional Diffusion Model Sampling
papers.summary: Stiff chemical kinetics is a major computational bottleneck in reacting-flow simulations, while data-driven solvers remain sensitive to training-state coverage and chemical dynamics. This work combines conditional diffusion sampling with a thermochemically constrained multiscale Laplace neural operator (TC-MLNO) for chemistry ODE integration. The diffusion model learns the equivalence-ratio-conditioned joint distribution of temperature and species from low-dimensional flame data, augmenting the state space without independent perturbations. TC-MLNO represents transient, non-periodic responses through pole-residue Laplace layers and assigns fast, medium, and slow species to separate branches. Thermochemical constraints are imposed through losses for mass and elemental conservation and heat release rate. The framework is evaluated in 1D premixed flames, a 2D developing jet, and a 3D turbulent burner flame. With equal-sized datasets, diffusion sampling reduces the 95th-percentile distance to the base flame manifold by up to 37.5% and the a posteriori full-species macro-average error by up to 92.7% versus random sampling, especially for minor species and radicals. TC-LNO yields smaller errors than the DeepONet baseline for 84.9% of retained modes and reduces the 95th-percentile error for the most attenuated modes from 0.372 to 0.081. In multidimensional flames, TC-MLNO better preserves reaction-zone locations, heat-release structures, and chemically sensitive species than DeepONet. Errors of representative radical and nitrogen-containing species in the 3D flame decrease by 88.0%-88.9%. Compared with direct CVODE integration, TC-MLNO reduces mean chemistry and total solution times by 90.1% and 62.6%, respectively. These results show that distribution-aware sampling and Laplace neural operator learning provide an accurate and efficient alternative for stiff chemical ODE integration.

papers.title: On magnetic-field consistency in the sideways force calculation of Phys. Plasmas 27, 012508 (2020)
papers.summary: We examine the consistency of the equilibrium magnetic field $\mathbf{B}_0$ used in the analytical calculation of the sideways wall force by A. A. Martynov and S. Yu. Medvedev [Phys. Plasmas 27, 012508 (2020)] and the subsequent reformulation presented in [Phys. Plasmas 27, 054702 (2020)]. In these attempts, the current density $\mathbf{j}_0 = \nabla \times \mathbf{B}_0$ must vanish in the vacuum regions adjacent to the wall, making $\mathbf{B}_0$ curl-free as a complement to the natural $\nabla \cdot \mathbf{B}_0 = 0$. Since the cited works incorporate selected toroidal corrections without explicitly specifying the corresponding differential operators, we test $\mathbf{B}_0$ adopted in these models against Maxwell's equations using both toroidal and quasi-cylindrical formulations. We show that the divergence-free requirement is violated in the toroidal interpretation, while the curl-free condition is not satisfied in the quasi-cylindrical limit. The reformulation likewise fails to define a self-consistent equilibrium field with toroidal effects because the accompanying field corrections required for consistency with Maxwell's equations are not specified. Since the sideways force calculations are built upon these inconsistent field prescriptions, their analytical derivations are consequently compromised. The resulting arguments therefore cannot serve as a valid basis for revising either the earlier results established by D. V. Mironov and V. D. Pustovitov [Phys. Plasmas 24, 092508 (2017)] or those obtained within the single-harmonic analysis [Phys. Plasmas 22, 052502 (2015)].

papers.title: Weber-number scaling and the distance dependence of drop size in full-cone pressure-swirl sprays
papers.summary: A pressure-swirl nozzle converts the feed pressure into a swirling conical sheet that breaks into ligaments and then into drops. The size of the drops governs the deposition and drift of agricultural sprays, the capture of airborne dust and the combustion efficiency of fuel injectors. The standard tool for measuring the drop size is laser diffraction, which returns a spatial, concentration-weighted distribution at the beam station. However, the dependence of the measured drop size on the nozzle-to-beam distance has not been quantified alongside a Weber-number scaling, so prefactors reported at different distances cannot be compared on an equal footing. To this end, we measure the drop-size distribution of two full-cone pressure-swirl nozzles by laser diffraction at a range of distances, pressures and orientations, together with high-speed imaging of the sheet breakup. We find that the volume-median diameter $D_{v50}$ decreases with the measurement distance $L$ as $D_{v50} \sim L^{-0.18}$ beyond the drop-formation region. A joint fit over both nozzles gives $D_{v50}/d_0 \sim \mathrm{We}^{-0.31}\,(L/d_0)^{-0.21}$, where $d_0$ is the orifice diameter and $\mathrm{We}$ the Weber number, which separates the pressure and distance effects. At a fixed distance the two nozzles collapse onto the $\mathrm{We}^{-1/3}$ scaling of Kooij et al. (2018), and the measured distance dependence may account for part of the offset between our near-field prefactor and the far-field value. Thus, a drop size obtained by laser diffraction is meaningful only when the measurement distance is reported with it, and a spray should be characterized at the actual distance between the nozzle and its target.

papers.title: An implicit multiscale solver for steady kinetic equations based on wave-particle decomposition
papers.summary: Steady kinetic computations require accurate transport on meshes that do not resolve the mean free path and efficient removal of slowly decaying macroscopic errors. We develop a closed wave-particle decomposition (WPD) and a residual-based implicit solver for this problem. The wave accumulates only the Maxwellian along a local characteristic horizon and is determined by the conservative variables; the particle carries the kinetic complement and collision remainder. Under moment compatibility, the closed system is equivalent to the kinetic equation. For the Bhatnagar-Gross-Krook and Shakhov models, a hydrodynamic expansion gives the wave and particle contributions to the Euler and Navier-Stokes fluxes. The implicit iteration couples macroscopic prediction to microscopic correction through a discrete endpoint term and synchronizes the conservative moments after each accepted correction. Its stationary states satisfy the target discrete kinetic equation independently of the iteration controls. Formal analysis gives the smooth fixed-mesh fluid limit. Linear model analysis relates convergence to the horizon-to-relaxation ratio, incomplete macroscopic solves and explicit collision remainders. One- and two-dimensional computations of a normal shock, internal flows and hypersonic external flows test these properties across rarefied and continuum regimes. The results show kinetic fidelity and substantial reductions in iteration counts and wall time relative to the conventional iterative scheme near the continuum limit. Collision-model comparisons and parameter studies support the predicted convergence mechanisms.

papers.title: Megabar Shocks on a Benchtop
papers.summary: Techniques to generate megabar (100 GPa) pressure are critical for the study of materials under extreme conditions. However, kJ-class lasers are typically needed to generate such extreme pressures. Here, we present a method to reach megabar pressure on a benchtop using only tens of mJ a few millijoules of laser pulse energy. The core of our method is the utilization of multiple laser rings of different diameters and time delays to additively excite a focusing shock wave. Using high-speed imaging and a streak camera, we measured the shock trajectory and inferred pressure, temperature and density using hydrocode simulation. Our shock compression efficiency, informed by hydrocode, has achieved 23 GPa/mJ. If scaled up, our method may enable high-energy-density experiments on a benchtop.

papers.title: Schr\"odinger's unpublished hidden-variable model in the 1944-45 debate over the "Collapse of Determinism"
papers.summary: In the mid-1940s, the question of whether quantum mechanics could be supplemented by deterministic hidden variables resurfaced in a debate in ^textit{Nature}. I show that Erwin Schr\"odinger drafted a hitherto unpublished response to this controversy. In it, Schr\"odinger provided an explicit hidden-variable model, thereby showing that such models could not be ruled out. I reconstruct the historical context of this forgotten manuscript and publish here the first transcription and analysis. Importantly, Schr\"odinger's proposal should be understood as a proof of principle rather than as evidence of his commitment to determinism.

papers.title: Platelet-driven contraction enlarges accessible space in layered fibrin networks without uniformly accelerating particle escape
papers.summary: Platelet traction contracts fibrin networks, yet whether contraction promotes or hinders the escape of suspended particles is unclear. We coupled an overdamped Langevin model of platelet--fibrin mechanics to Brownian transport of finite-size tracers through frozen network states. Nine mechanical replicas were evolved at four filopodial traction baselines (0--8.8\,nN), stacked into 5-$\mu$m-thick domains of 50 layers and probed at 0--15\,s with 0.5-$\mu$m tracers (29,952 trajectories, 100\,s observation). Benchmarked against experimental clot-contraction kinetics, the simulated contraction is post-lag, within one order of magnitude of experimental rates and corresponds to the onset of the contraction phase. Relative to the matched zero-baseline control, every active-baseline state showed greater projected contraction and a larger tracer-accessible volume ($+9.3\%$ to $+27.6\%$; exact sign test $p=0.0039$ per condition). At 15\,s, mean survival at 100\,s fell from 27.3\% to 14.3\% and the restricted mean exit time from 56.5 to 44.0\,s between the lowest and highest baseline, and all nine replicas shortened residence at 8.8\,nN. At lower baselines, responses differed among replicas, and nearly all retained tracers with a classified start were connected to an exit. Contraction therefore enlarges accessible space without uniformly accelerating escape, separating geometric accommodation from transport kinetics.

papers.title: Pumping by Two-frequency Steady Streaming: Impact of Amplitude Ratio and Phase
papers.summary: The classical phenomenon of steady streaming around a circular cylinder oscillating with a single frequency results in a symmetric quadrupole-like flow structure. In [H.S.\ Lee, \textit{et al.}, J.\ Fluid Mech.\ 1038, A34 (2026)], we demonstrated using asymptotic analysis and numerical simulations that a cylinder vibrating with two frequencies yields asymmetrical steady streaming that pumps the fluid in one direction. The asymptotic expansion at small amplitude showed that pumping occurs at third order or higher depending on the frequency ratio, but the solutions are analytically intractable and the influence of key control parameters, like the amplitude ratio and phase difference, remained undetermined. Here, we analyze two-frequency steady streaming on an annular domain and reduce the equations from the asymptotic expansion to a series of boundary value problems of one spatial dimension, which can be numerically solved efficiently. For frequency ratio 2, we show that the net force on the cylinder is proportional to $\cos(\phi - \phi^*(\text{Re}))\beta/ (1+\beta^2)^{3/2}$, where $\beta$ is the amplitude ratio, $\phi$ is the phase difference, Re is the Reynolds number, and $\phi^*(\text{Re})$ is the phase that gives the largest force. To test whether the force on an enclosed annulus serves as a useful proxy for pumping in an open system, we also performed numerical simulations of a cylinder oscillating with two-frequencies in a rectangular channel. Our computations demonstrate that the net flux through the channel is directly proportional to the net force on the annulus over all parameter ranges tested. Finally, we discuss the implications for using two-frequency oscillations to pump fluid in lab-on-a-chip and other devices.

papers.title: Building and calibrating a 3Di subgrid flood model for Hanoi, without a surveyed terrain model, drainage data, or rain gauges
papers.summary: Urban hydrodynamic flood models typically rely on a surveyed terrain model, an explicit pipe drainage network, and rain gauge measurements, none of which were available for the inundation following Typhoon Matmo in My Dinh and Tay Mo, Hanoi, on 7 October 2025. The present study addresses this issue by documenting the construction and calibration of a 32.8 km^2 3Di subgrid model under severe data constraints, demonstrating how unmonitored catchments can be simulated using openly accessible sources. Specifically, a 1 m digital elevation model was systematically repaired for river and lake bathymetry, unsurveyed water bodies, road underpasses, and an excavation pit to re-establish essential overland flow paths. In addition, assigned infiltration rates across land-cover classes were utilized to stand in for the unrecorded subsurface sewer system, while half-hourly satellite precipitation from the IMERG Late product provided rainfall forcing for a closed two-dimensional domain. Model calibration was conducted against eight crowdsourced depth observations. The simulation results demonstrated that six observation points retained surface water and were closely aligned with the reported values within 2.2 cm. However, two peripheral locations along Tay Mo Road and Road 70 remained completely dry in the model. Because all eight points were utilized during parameter adjustment and no independent validation dataset was withheld, this correspondence reflects a calibration fit rather than an unconstrained predictive test.

papers.title: A Rydberg atom array coupled to a high-cooperativity optical cavity
papers.summary: Integrating Rydberg-state control of atom-atom interactions with cavity control of atom-light interactions enables the combination of local entangling operations with photon-mediated long-range coupling, measurement, and communication. Such integration is challenging because electric fields generated by charges on cavity optics and by cavity-stabilizing actuators may disturb Rydberg-state coherence. Here, we couple a Rydberg tweezer array to a high-cooperativity optical cavity, suppressing the electric fields produced by cavity length actuation so that the residual field variation of about $3~\mathrm{mV/cm}$ rms does not limit Rydberg coherence. We demonstrate two capabilities that neither system provides alone. First, we use Purcell-enhanced fluorescence to read out atoms directly in the ground-Rydberg basis within $7.5~\mu\mathrm{s}$, well within the Rydberg-state lifetime, with ground- and Rydberg-state detection infidelities of $3\%$ and $5\%$, respectively, and with low atom loss. Second, we use Rydberg-Rydberg interactions to control collective light-atom scattering into the cavity mode. Specifically, we drive blockaded Rabi oscillations between a state with two ground-state atoms, which scatter collectively with a superradiant or subradiant rate controlled by the atomic positions, and an entangled state with a single Rydberg excitation, which scatters like a single atom. These capabilities open routes toward networked Rydberg processors, mid-circuit measurements in analog quantum simulators, and many-body quantum optics with entangled emitters coupled collectively to light.

papers.title: Vibrational Dressing of Collective Molecular Polaritons: A Scalable Green's-Function Theory
papers.summary: We develop a scalable Green's-function theory of vibrationally dressed molecular-polariton absorption in the Holstein--Tavis--Cummings model. Within the self-consistent Born approximation (SCBA), the ground-state linear response of $N$ identical molecules coupled to one cavity mode follows from a $2\times2$ cavity--bright matrix, while scattering through the $N-1$ dark states remains in the molecular self-energy. The number of self-consistent equations is independent of $N$, allowing large ensembles to be treated without explicitly resolving the dark manifold. Benchmarks against hierarchical equations of motion show that the theory captures collective linewidth narrowing and an $N$-dependent minimum in the lower-polariton linewidth as its exciton fraction varies, beyond a Hopfield-weighted linewidth estimate. Comparisons with exact diagonalization for discrete local vibrations show weaker vibronic progressions and better overall SCBA agreement as $N$ increases at fixed single-molecule coupling. The resulting framework connects microscopic vibrational scattering to collective absorption spectra without introducing fitted polariton linewidths.

papers.title: Analytically Benchmarked Spatial and Temporal Discretization Guidelines for Finite Element Simulation of Thermal Waves
papers.summary: Finite element simulation is widely used to design and interpret thermal wave-based measurement systems. The accuracy of the results obtained from such simulations depends on how finely the model is resolved in space and time. The discretization resolution is often chosen case by case rather than following a well-defined guideline. This work recommends a discretization protocol for finite element simulation of thermal waves where the spatial discretization is scaled to the thermal diffusion length and the temporal discretization to the number of time steps per cycle. The associated discretization errors are quantified using three benchmark problems of increasing complexity. The spatial phase error converges at second order in the element size, reaching 0.14 degrees at ten elements per diffusion length, whereas the temporal error decreases only at first order in the number of time steps per cycle; thus, the time step can be set from a target phase tolerance $\epsilon$. Each error is assessed against a reference that isolates it. The benchmark case with subsurface defects shows the consequence of violating the recommended discretization protocol.

papers.title: A differentiable PCA-GPR surrogate framework for full-transient Bayesian inverse uncertainty quantification of black-box nuclear thermal-hydraulic systems
papers.summary: Complex transient energy systems require uncertainty-quantified predictions, but Bayesian inverse uncertainty quantification (IUQ) is often impractical because posterior sampling with high-fidelity system codes requires many expensive full-transient simulations. This study develops a surrogate-assisted Bayesian IUQ framework that makes full-time-series calibration practical for the NACIE heavy-liquid-metal natural-circulation loop. The key innovation is to transform a black-box transient simulator into a differentiable probabilistic emulator by combining principal component analysis with Gaussian process regression (PCA--GPR). The surrogate reconstructs complete multichannel temperature and mass-flow histories from a compact latent representation, preserving dominant temporal and cross-channel correlations while enabling automatic differentiation of the log posterior. This allows both gradient-free ensemble slice sampling and gradient-informed sampling with the No-U-Turn Sampler and Microcanonical Langevin Monte Carlo. Five principal components capture more than 99\% of the output variance, and the surrogate achieves normalized root-mean-square errors below 2\%. Compared with direct Flownex SE evaluations, the surrogate reduces likelihood-evaluation cost by approximately 3000-fold while preserving posterior statistics and correlations. Posterior predictive analyses show reduced bias, narrower intervals, and improved agreement with measurements and independent validation.

papers.title: Variable Masking for Climate Emulation in ACE
papers.summary: In the recent AI Model Intercomparison Project (AIMIP) benchmark, the ACE2.1-ERA5 emulator was shown to underestimate the true near-surface warming trend both during the training period and the out-of-sample extrapolation period. We show that M-ACE2S improves long-term near-surface air temperature prediction. We also present a novel data normalization strategy called "global mean removal", which, combined with masking, further improves the near-surface temperature forecasts. We show that M-ACE2S outperforms the ACE2S baseline on in-sample data for ERA5 while improving training stability and generalizability of near-surface temperature to unseen forcing when paired with global mean removal.

papers.title: Localized high-Q resonances enable electrically defined beam steering in lithium niobate metasurfaces
papers.summary: High-speed beam steering for LiDAR and optical communication requires independent, reconfigurable control of optical phase. We demonstrate a metasurface combining lithium niobate's Pockels effect with high-Q (Q > 1700) silicon guided-mode resonance nanoantennas whose localized resonances allow individual electro-optic control at a 1 $\mu$m pitch. Identical arrays steer light to 53.5$^\circ$ or 32.4$^\circ$, with the angle set by the bias pattern rather than antenna geometry. We measure 18.0% 0th-order modulation depth, 0.09% of incident power in the steered order, and a 940 MHz detected modulation bandwidth. Mode-overlap analysis shows how inter-element coupling limits usable Q, providing design rules for compact, high-speed beam steering.

papers.title: A Scalable Sharp-Interface Immersed Boundary Method for Moving Boundary Flow Simulation on Multi-GPU Systems
papers.summary: Sharp-interface immersed boundary methods provide a versatile framework for simulating flows with complex moving boundaries, but their irregular data structures, dynamic sparsity, and discontinuous pressure operators present significant challenges for efficient multi-GPU implementation. This work presents a fully GPU-native, multi-GPU acceleration of the sharp-interface immersed boundary solver, ViCar3D. The implementation combines a hybrid OpenACC/CUDA programming model with a matrix decomposition that isolates dynamically changing immersed-boundary operators, GPU-optimized geometric kernels, asynchronous dual-stream sparse matrix--vector execution, and a symmetric-memory-based sparse communication strategy. A GPU-oriented iterative solver employing a preconditioned stabilized bi-conjugate gradient (BiCGStab) method is developed to efficiently treat the pressure Poisson equation on highly stretched Cartesian grids. The resulting framework preserves the accuracy and versatility of the original solver while delivering substantial acceleration and scalability for simulations involving complex moving and deforming immersed boundaries, thereby extending the applicability of sharp-interface immersed boundary methods to extreme-scale computational fluid dynamics.

papers.title: Data-Driven Optimization of Seminumerical Exchange for SIMD CPUs
papers.summary: We present a seminumerical exchange algorithm (SNK) based on the sn-LinK method [Laqua et al., J. Chem. Theory Comput. 16, 1456 (2020)], optimized for modern multi-core central processing units with single instruction multiple data vector instructions and report its implementation into the Q-Chem quantum chemistry program. Vectorization and memory management strategies for the Boys function and 3-center-1-electron (3c1e) integral kernels are given. Several new considerations are made in the computation of the 3c1e integrals: the Head-Gordon Pople horizontal recurrence relations, same-center optimizations, and multishell optimizations, all implemented symbolically employing the SymPy symbolic algebra library and exported as optimized C++ code leveraging common-sub-expression elimination (CSE) optimization techniques. A general scheme for choosing optimal integral kernels is developed through rigorous timing benchmarks. The resulting implementation is tested against traditional 4c2e exchange for several systems and basis sets, showing 1-2 orders of magnitude speedups for systems of practically relevant sizes (100-500 atoms, 2000-10000 basis functions). For smaller molecules, comparisons are also made against the more efficient occ-RI-K method showing a break-even point around 50-100 atoms beyond which SNK dramatically outperforms due to its superior sub-quadratic (between linear and quadratic) time complexity as well as its effectively negligible memory demand.

papers.title: Aluminum wide-range EOS sensitivity in Z-pinch dynamic-hohlraum liner-foam impact and outgoing radiation
papers.summary: In a Z-pinch dynamic hohlraum, an aluminum liner collides with a central foam and converts kinetic energy into radiation, and the liner-foam response depends on the aluminum equation of state (EOS). We construct a wide-range aluminum equation-of-state table from density functional theory (DFT) simulations over solid-liquid-plasma regions, denoted DFT-eos. Mixed deterministic-stochastic finite-temperature DFT (mDFT) gives the electron thermal contribution; quantum molecular dynamics (QMD) with classical calibration gives the ion part. We perform one-dimensional cylindrical radiation magnetohydrodynamics (MHD) simulations at a peak current of 50 MA and rise times of 220-300 ns on a single-layer light foam load. Opacity and electrical conductivity are fixed; only the liner Al EOS is changed between DFT-eos and the quotidian EOS (QEOS). Impact time and peak liner kinetic energy change little between the two tables. Larger differences appear in flight-segment density, the contact state at impact, and the time history of outgoing radiation power at the outer interface.

papers.title: Constrained Nuclear-Electronic Orbital Time-Dependent Density Functional Theory for Excited-State Dynamics with Nuclear Quantum Effects
papers.summary: Nuclear quantum effects can strongly influence excited-state processes involving light nuclei, yet their inclusion in practical molecular dynamics remains challenging. We develop constrained nuclear-electronic orbital time-dependent density functional theory (CNEO-TDDFT), which incorporates quantum-nuclear delocalization into full-dimensional effective excited-state potential energy surfaces while retaining the formal structure and computational scaling of conventional TDDFT. Analytic gradients are also developed, enabling efficient on-the-fly excited-state dynamics. CNEO-TDDFT substantially improves excited-state vibrational frequencies involving hydrogen motion and reduces the root-mean-square deviation from experiment from 113 cm$^{-1}$ to 26 cm$^{-1}$. For excited-state proton transfer in 10-hydroxybenzo[h]quinoline (HBQ), CNEO-TDDFT yields a characteristic transfer time of 14.0 fs, compared with 25.5 fs from conventional TDDFT, consistent with the experimentally inferred ultrafast timescale of 12$\pm$6 fs. These results establish CNEO-TDDFT as an accurate and efficient framework for excited-state dynamics with nuclear quantum effects.

papers.title: A Panoramic Network Overview of Shortcut Impact on Power Grids
papers.summary: Synchronization of coupled oscillators on complex networks underlies critical functions in natural and engineered systems, including power-grid operation. While synchronization stability on fixed network topologies has been studied extensively, less is known about how an added transmission link affects stability depending on where it is placed relative to generation and consumption. We address this question using simplified ring-network power-grid models in which producer and consumer nodes are spatially organized into clusters. Long-range transmission links, which we refer to as shortcuts, are added between non-adjacent nodes, and synchronization stability is quantified by basin stability in second-order coupled-oscillator dynamics. We compare shortcut placements across four scenarios varying network size, power allocation, power-injection heterogeneity, and producer--consumer arrangement. When producers and consumers form two spatially separated clusters, center-to-center shortcuts do not reduce the mean basin stability in the configurations examined and increase it by up to 75\% relative to the shortcut-less baseline. Peripheral shortcuts instead reduce mean basin stability by up to 28\% in some configurations despite the added connection, producing Braess-like degradation. In alternating multi-block networks, however, no single shortcut placement provides the same substantial enhancement, indicating that the center-to-center advantage does not directly generalize to more complex spatial arrangements. Representative time-domain simulations further show faster decay of frequency deviations for center-to-center than for peripheral shortcuts. These results demonstrate that the effect of added connectivity depends critically on where the new link is placed relative to the spatial organization of generation and consumption.

papers.title: Energy Flow Shapes the Decomposition Dynamics of a Reactive Atmospheric Intermediate
papers.summary: The unimolecular dynamics of Criegee intermediates depend strongly on their internal energy, which can differ substantially between nascent atmospheric species and laboratory-prepared reactants. Here, the decomposition dynamics of {\it anti-}CH$_3$CHOO are investigated using molecular dynamics simulations on a neural network-based potential energy surface under thermal and mode-selective vibrational excitation. Simulations were performed at internal energies representative of those released during ozonolysis (chemical/thermal preparation, TP) or following vibrational excitation (VibEx) along the CH-stretching mode with two or three quanta, as can be done in laboratory studies. These excitation conditions strongly affect reaction yields and kinetics, with VibEx promoting passage across the initial cyclization barrier. For TP, 35 kcal/mol of internal energy are required to form molecular products, whereas for VibEx, 27 kcal/mol are sufficient. Although TP and VibEx ensembles access largely the same fragmentation pathways with comparable relative yields, the absolute product yields, characteristic timescales, and kinetic behavior differ substantially. Methyldioxirane is found to be a kinetic trap along the pathway. The resulting molecular-level description of {\it anti-}CH$_3$CHOO decomposition provides guidance for interpreting experiments and contributes to a broader understanding of energy-dependent Criegee-intermediate dynamics.

papers.title: RAT-EC: Introducing a New Open-Source 3D Volume-Integral Eddy-Current Module
papers.summary: We present RAT-EC, an open-source volume-integral eddy-current module for unstructured meshes, driven in the time domain by coils of arbitrary winding geometry. It is the first openly available code of this kind and part of the open-source RAT suite. Because only the conductor is meshed, neither the surrounding air nor an artificial outer boundary has to be modelled, which simplifies model preparation and brings problems with thin gaps and intricate air regions within reach of standard hardware. The formulation combines a semi-analytical evaluation of the singular and near-singular inductance terms, a multi-level fast multipole method that accelerates both the far-field inductance action and the coil field, topology-aware constraints for multiply connected conductors, and a matrix-free, GPU-accelerated time integration. The implementation is verified against closed-form solutions for a conducting sphere and a conducting ring, and is validated on the TEAM-7 benchmark. At 50 Hz, RAT-EC reproduces the measured field as accurately as finite-element solutions. At 200 Hz, it agrees with a converged finite-element model, but both deviate from published measurements, which suggests that this benchmark point should be re-examined. RAT-EC provides an open platform for volume-integral eddy-current simulation and method development.

papers.title: Monte Carlo Framework for Physics-Based Design and Optimization of X-Ray Compressive Ghost Imaging Systems
papers.summary: X-ray ghost imaging has emerged as a promising computational imaging modality capable of forming images from spatially integrated measurements. Unlike optical implementations, image formation is governed by multiple energy-dependent photon-matter interactions: photoelectric absorption, Compton scattering, and fluorescence. The relative contributions of these interactions depend on the source spectrum, sample geometry and composition, and detector configuration. We present a FLUKA-based Monte Carlo framework that models photon transport and predicts bucket signals generated by binary illumination patterns. The framework couples a physical scaling analysis, which converts the simulated bucket signals into photon numbers, tube loading and absorbed dose, with a ghost imaging reconstruction analysis of image quality and convergence. Our framework helps assess whether a given configuration is limited by the source output, the mask modulation or the reconstruction before any measurement is made. We evaluate the reconstruction for a centimeter-scale imaging system for an iron crown using one transmission detector and three off-axis scattering detectors over a range of source spectra. The results reveal how source characteristics and detector geometry influence reconstruction quality and radiation dose, providing quantitative guidelines for future X-ray ghost imaging system design. More broadly, this work establishes a predictive design framework for application-specific X-ray ghost imaging systems.

papers.title: Nonreciprocal Control of Spatiotemporal Floquet Dynamics in Levitated Optomechanical Arrays
papers.summary: Periodically driven photonic and optomechanical systems provide a versatile setting for realizing collective Floquet dynamics, yet the relation between temporal locking and continuous rotation of the finite-$q$ pattern remains poorly understood. We show that a nonreciprocal ring of parametrically driven optically levitated particles allows the spatial phase to be controlled while collective temporal locking is preserved. Nonreciprocity polarizes the counterpropagating finite-wave-vector modes and drives a transition from the pinned state to persistent directional spatial-phase drift. The normalized spatial-phase drift velocity is independently encoded in the splitting of the two dominant spectral branches, and its direction reverses with the coupling asymmetry. The pinned regime exhibits a laboratory frame period-two time-crystalline response, whereas the rotating regime forms a distinct temporally locked spatiotemporally ordered state. The same correspondence between spatial-phase drift and spectral splitting persists down to few-particle rings, indicating that the effect does not require a large array. These results establish nonreciprocity as a route to independently control spatial-phase drift and temporal synchronization in driven levitated optomechanical systems.

papers.title: Machine Learning Surrogate Model for Accelerating InGaAs/GaAs Quantum Well Laser Design
papers.summary: A machine-learning surrogate model based on a multi-layer perceptron neural network is used to predict six laser performance metrics for an indium gallium arsenide quantum well laser given epitaxial layer parameters as inputs. The surrogate model was trained on simulation data from a set of 4999 designs which were generated by varying epitaxial layer parameters and simulating each design with Harold to extract performance metrics. The model predicts all 6 chosen metrics with a coefficient of determination, $R^2$, greater than 0.91 on a held-out test set and demonstrates a $\sim 10^6 \times$ speed up compared to full device simulations. The model is used to search across 1 million potential epitaxial designs in the parameter space and find designs that minimize threshold current and internal loss. Using the surrogate, rather than full device simulation, reduces computation time for a million designs from 231 days to $\sim$2 minutes on a standard laptop. It is also demonstrated that use of the Swish activation function, rather than ReLU, together with engineered input features - i.e. derived quantities calculated from the base model inputs - raise the mean $R^2$ from 0.88 to 0.94 without additional training data, and reduce the mean absolute percentage error from $1.78 \pm 0.08 \%$ to $1.17 \pm 0.09 \%$.

papers.title: Space Sustainability: The Global Commons
papers.summary: Space is no longer a distant, barely reachable frontier of scientific exploration; it has become a critical infrastructure for life on Earth and a rapidly expanding zone of intense commercial activity. Yet this expansion is unfolding in ways that replicate, and amplify, the unsustainable dynamics already driving ecological and social crises on our planet. This chapter explains the concept of space sustainability as a multidimensional challenge; it raises the questions of governance, knowledge, power, justice, and global responsibility. It highlights both the profound benefits derived from space activities and the uneven distribution of costs and risks, from orbital debris and atmospheric impacts to privatization of essential services. We therefore argue that it frames space as a global commons that demands stewardship rather than pure exploitation, cooperation rather than competition, and governance that prioritizes long-term wellbeing rather than laissez-faire approach. Sustainability in space is inseparable from sustainability on Earth. This chapter invites readers, whether they are space administration and industry actors, policymakers, scientists, or simply engaged citizens, to see space not as a limitless frontier, but as a shared domain whose future depends on collective choices made today.

papers.title: Quantitative validation of SMBI deposition profiles on EAST using experimentally constrained simulations
papers.summary: Quantitative comparison between SMBI fueling simulations and experiments has long been hampered by the poor constraint on the effective source. Here, the particle increment per pulse is extracted experimentally and used to calibrate the simulation source. For EAST shot 71438, the density evolution from microwave reflectometry is analyzed for nine SMBI pulse groups. The SMBI-induced density increase is isolated from the background by comparing the rising and falling phases around each pulse group. Its radial profile peaks in the mid-pedestal region for every pulse group. Volume integration of this increment provides the experimental reference. The simulations use a multi-fluid model in the BOUT++ framework in which two transport operators are recast into conservative flux form, with the particle balance residual reduced to about 2% of the injected amount, and the perpendicular transport coefficients are constructed from the discrete radial flux balance, with the unphysical changes of the initial density and temperature profiles in source-free evolution reduced by an order of magnitude. For three cases sharing the same nominal molecular flux, the simulated deposition peak agrees with the experimental one in the relative pedestal coordinate. The simulated conversion of the injected particles at the end of the injection is slightly lower than the value inferred from the experiment, while the fraction retained at the end of the pulse is higher. The perturbation thus decays more slowly in the simulation, which we attribute to fast loss channels not represented in the model, such as parallel losses to the scrape-off layer. The edge electron temperature stays on the high-temperature plateau of the dissociation and ionization rate coefficients throughout the pulse, and the inward shift of the deposition with edge cooling reported earlier does not occur under the present conditions.

papers.title: Mobility energetic balance frames spatial configuration of cities
papers.summary: Urban spatial configurations emerge as the result of interactions between citizens' activities, movements and the landscape. Topography forms part of the physical settings through which mobility occurs, influencing movement energetic requirements. Using road networks, elevation data and mobility flows inferred from geolocated records, we define a simplified comparative measure of movement energy and test how it changes when the observed urban configuration is translated, rotated or rescaled within its topographic setting while mobility demand is held fixed. Across 56 cities, observed configurations consistently show lower movement energy requirements than most of the alternative configurations examined. This recurrent pattern reveals a measurable relationship between topography and urban spatial organization and is compatible with cumulative adaptation among urban structure, mobility and terrain. These findings add an energetic dimension to our understanding of how topography relates to urban spatial organization and provide an empirical basis for considering terrain-related movement requirements when evaluating future urban growth and densification.

papers.title: Effect of leading edge geometry on aerodynamic performance of a flat plate
papers.summary: Flow separation around flat plate is influenced by the thickness and leading edge geometry, which creates the shear stresses and pressure distribution manifesting into unsteady aerodynamic forces. Leading edge geometries have been widely reported but the influence of leading edge curvature at low Reynolds numbers (Re) have found less attention. The present study uses two dimensional numerical simulation to investigate the effect of a hemispherical curvature (protuberance) at the leading edge and reports how vortex shedding, shedding frequencies and aerodynamic forces are affected over a range of angles of attack ($0^\circ \leq \alpha \leq 25^\circ$) at Re = 1000. Thicker vortical regions are formed near the plate with curvature at the leading edge. Onset of shedding is noted at angle of attack of $5^\circ$ for the plate with curvature at the leading edge and it gets delayed for simple flat plate. The temporal force coefficients on the plates show multiple frequencies at higher angles of attack. The plate with curvature at the leading edge has a glide ratio of 1 at $0^\circ$ angle of attack and has equivalent glide ratio to that of simple flat plate at higher angles of attack. The simple flat plate has better glide ratios at moderate angles of attack like $5^\circ, 10^\circ$ and $15^\circ$. The results will help in making engineering informed design decisions for smaller unmanned aerial/aquatic vehicles cruising at low Reynolds numbers.

papers.title: Fast, parallel, three-dimensional rearrangement of atom arrays using superpositions of elementary holograms
papers.summary: Assembling defect-free arrays of neutral atoms requires real-time rearrangement of stochastically loaded optical tweezers. Conventional rearrangement methods shuttle atoms sequentially, whereas high-speed spatial light modulators (SLMs) can move all atoms in parallel, which scales more favorably as the array size grows. For fast parallel rearrangement, the sequence of holograms displayed on the SLM should be computed more rapidly than the SLM refresh rate, and there should be phase continuity between successive holograms to minimize transient intensity fluctuations. We calculate holograms analytically by adding together the complex fields needed to produce each individual trap, and we ramp the phase of each trap linearly as it moves to its target location. Trap positions enter as continuous variables, rather than tied to points on a grid, so the method provides high positioning accuracy. Using a single GPU, we compute each intermediate hologram in 0.284 ms, considerably faster than the SLM refresh time of 0.696 ms, so the rearrangement speed is hardware-limited. In each step, we use the free processing time to iteratively optimize the holograms for equal intensity across the traps, decreasing trap non-uniformity to 1.24% during rearrangement at no cost in total time. Starting from an array of 256 sites loaded stochastically with $^{87}$Rb atoms, we assemble a 100-atom array in under 20 ms with a rearrangement survival probability of 99.31(12)% per atom. This rearrangement increases the temperature of the atoms by 9(3) $\mu$K, which is small compared to the trap depth of 480 $\mu$K. Our method can also move individual atoms axially, enabling transport in different planes. We demonstrate this capability with a rearrangement protocol where one set of atoms leapfrogs over another.

papers.title: Popularity-driven interactions in multilayer bounded-confidence opinion dynamics
papers.summary: Social media users interact with their own social networks but also with platform-wide content, where a small number of highly popular users may receive a disproportionate share of attention. In this paper, we study how those interactions outside the social networks and user popularity regulate the formation of opinion clusters. We design a bounded-confidence opinion dynamics model on a multilayer network consisting of a social network coupled to a fully connected explore layer of potential interaction contacts. We show that uniform sampling on the explore layer increases mixing across social neighbourhoods and reduces opinion diversity while also weakening the influence of the underlying social network. We then introduce a popularity-driven interaction mechanism in which contact selection is biased by a time-evolving popularity score, so that frequently selected users become increasingly likely to be re-selected. The resulting concentration of explore-layer interactions on a small number of highly popular users reduces the homogenising effect of the explore layer, increasing opinion diversity. The resulting changes relative to a single-layer system depend on the underlying social network structure. As the popularity inequality increases, a small number of highly popular users can act as opinion attractors and sustain polarisation in regimes where the corresponding model without popularity heterogeneity converges to consensus.

papers.title: Reliability-Aware Refinement of High-Resolution Human Mobility Origin-Destination Tables under Sparsity and Suppression
papers.summary: High-resolution origin-destination (OD) tables derived from digital mobility traces can preserve fine-scale collective movement structure, but sampling, population expansion, and privacy-motivated low-count suppression create heterogeneous observational support across OD entries and make apparent zeros difficult to interpret. We develop a reliability-aware refinement framework that combines each released OD entry with a time-resolved, data-informed radiation baseline through a closed-form cell-wise Gamma-Poisson update, without smoothing neighboring OD pairs. Applied to a 125 m hourly Tokyo OD product, the method preserves concentrated directional flows while adding lower-intensity, baseline-supported links. The relative contribution of released and model-supported structure varies substantially across OD pairs and departure hours, including among positive-flow entries: released flows are most strongly retained at 7:00, followed by 17:00, whereas the radiation baseline contributes more at 13:00. The inferred characteristic radius broadens the movement range represented by the baseline and exhibits structured variation around major station areas and rail corridors. Tokyo and Fukuoka also show a common increase in data-baseline separation at long distances. Under controlled Poisson thinning, calibrated refinement yields lower realization-averaged mean absolute error than an independently resampled no-refinement table across the tested conditions. This experiment provides internal calibration under imposed degradation, not external validation against true unsuppressed flows. The framework thus provides a transparent way to preserve fine-scale empirical mobility structure while making the cell-wise contribution of structured model support explicit.

papers.title: Acoustic Illusion of a Rigid Object for a Moving Emitter via Equivalent Surface Control
papers.summary: We report a three-dimensional acoustic illusion of a rigid object illuminated by an emitter moving along an arbitrary trajectory. The object is absent: control sources are arranged around its location, the closed surface they define being termed the equivalent surface. Driven by the field the object would have scattered onto this surface, the sources radiate, by the Kirchhoff--Helmholtz representation, that same field beyond it. The control signals follow in closed form from a time-dependent physical optics formulation that we derive for a moving emitter, in which the motion enters analytically through the acoustic travel times, so that the scattering problem need not be re-solved at each emitter position, nor the propagation domain discretized. For objects too large to enclose, the signals are mapped onto an internal surface, an option whose advantages and penalties are discussed. Numerical simulations validate the method in both configurations.

papers.title: Effect of deuteration on methane cluster stability
papers.summary: The evaporation from clusters of mixed deuterated and protonated methane molecules has been studied experimentally and theoretically. Only loss of the two components CH$_4$ and CD$_4$ is observed, showing the absence of hydrogen scrambling. The branching ratio of the two channels scales with the mole fractions of the isotopologues, corresponding to a fixed ratio of 1.5 for the CH$_4$ and CD$_4$ rates. The number is explained by the combined effect of the zero-point energies found in quantum chemical calculations and the use of detailed balance to describe the evaporation process, the latter by incorporating the moment of inertia of the two isotopologue molecules and their rotational degrees of freedom. The difference in evaporative activation energies is determined to be 6.1~\% and 6.8~\% from two experimental determinations and 8.7~\% theoretically with B3LYP+GD3BJ, corresponding to 5--7~meV. The same theory finds the CH$_4$ activation energy to be 83.8 meV, close to the experimental bulk value of 84.7 meV. Differences in Helmholtz free energies of decay products are extracted from the experimental data, yielding the molecular mixing as the only contribution to the entropy term.

papers.title: Hurricane Laura-induced loads on wind turbines -- Part I: High-fidelity modeling and sensitivity to turbulent inflow conditions
papers.summary: Tropical cyclones can produce extreme winds in the lowest portion of the boundary layer, posing high risks to critical energy infrastructure, including wind energy systems. This study evaluates the dynamic response of an idling wind turbine to turbulent inflow generated during the passage of a hurricane. We performed large-eddy simulations of Hurricane Laura (2020) at several grid resolutions -- coarse $(\Delta x=55.55\,{\rm m})$, intermediate $(\Delta x=25\,{\rm m})$, and fine $(\Delta x=10\,{\rm m})$ -- to investigate differences in mean flow characteristics and turbulence structures as the hurricane progresses across a virtual wind turbine location. The large-eddy simulation data served as direct inflow conditions for aeroelastic simulations to assess the turbine's response. Our results reveal significant differences in the mean wind and turbulent flow structures between the grid resolutions, leading to distinct impacts on the wind turbine's aeroelastic behavior. These findings emphasize the need for high-resolution inflow information to better predict extreme loads and inform the design of wind turbines in regions frequently affected by tropical cyclones. As a continuation of this work, Part II of this study will evaluate the turbine's response from different locations relative to the storm's trajectory and compare it with current wind turbine design practices.

papers.title: Thermal Confinement in Plasmonic Nanoparticles under Generalised Pulsed Illumination
papers.summary: Thermal confinement is a key parameter in photothermal applications, as it determines the spatial extent of the region affected by the generated heat. In this work, we develop a numerical treatment to quantify thermal confinement in spherical plasmonic nanoparticles under excitation conditions ranging from ultrashort pulses to the continuous-wave regime. The model combines generalized optical heating with a finite-difference solution of the transient heat equation and explicitly accounts for finite interfacial thermal conductance. To characterize the spatial distribution of heat, we introduce a thermal confinement radius defined from the temporal temperature envelope in the surrounding medium. We demonstrate that pulse duration acts as a highly effective, tuneable parameter to govern thermal confinement. Notably, we quantitatively show that finite interfacial thermal conductance can induce deviations of up to 20% in the spatial confinement radius and over 60% in the transient thermal construct under ultrashort excitation. By comparing the characteristic dimensions of representative targeting ligands with the resulting thermal-confinement length scales, we show how pulse duration can be precisely tailored to control target heating. These results provide a unified framework for predicting nanoscale heat localization paving the way for the rational design of high precision thermoplasmonic applications.

papers.title: From Algebraic Completeness to Orbit Separation: Recursive Separating Invariants for Global Neural Network Potential Energy Surfaces
papers.summary: Permutationally invariant polynomials (PIPs) provide a systematically improvable, symmetry-preserving representation for global potential energy surfaces (PESs), but their high computational cost as neural network descriptors limits applications to large molecular systems. Fundamental invariants (FIs), which form an algebraically complete generating set, substantially reduce the number of descriptors and enable neural network PESs for larger systems. However, PES evaluation remains computationally expensive as molecular size and complexity increase. Here, we introduce recursive separating invariants (RSIs), shifting the descriptor design principle from algebraic completeness to orbit separation. RSIs are constructed systematically through correlation order and recursion depth, providing a more computationally efficient representation. Benchmarks on reactive and nonreactive systems demonstrate that RSI-based neural network (RSI-NN) PESs achieve approximately an order-of-magnitude faster evaluation than their FI-NN counterparts, with system-dependent prediction accuracy that is comparable in several cases. These results establish orbit separation as a promising principle for developing efficient symmetry-preserving descriptors for global neural network PESs.

papers.title: Correlation between normal character and Raman intensities of isotopologues of carbon dioxide
papers.summary: Previous studies on the vibrational structure of carbon dioxide isotopologues have revealed a correlation between the strength of Fermi interactions and a recently defined normal-mode parameter. In this contribution, we investigate how the Raman intensities of the most intense bands evolve across the complete series of carbon dioxide isotopologues at room temperature. To this end, we introduce a general scheme for simulating Raman intensities in linear triatomic molecules, based on the computation of the mean polarizability surface up to cubic terms for all twelve stable species. For the first time, we establish correlations between the degree of normality and the Raman transition intensities, mean polarizability derivatives, and variational Raman shift errors across the CO$_2$ isotopologue series. The observed trends are further analyzed by considering rotational contributions, which may partially account for the deviations observed in the correlations. Our study is supported by experimental Raman spectra of isotopically enriched samples and theoretical simulations. Although this study focuses on carbon dioxide, similar behavior is expected for other series of isotopologues.

papers.title: Watt-level single-cavity dual-comb laser at 2.1 $\mu$m wavelength
papers.summary: Compact ultrafast laser combs around the 2 $\mu$m atmospheric transmission window are of growing interest for direct spectroscopy and as drivers for nonlinear conversion to otherwise hard-to-reach spectral regions. Dual-comb systems in this region remain very scarce: existing implementations rely mostly on nonlinear conversion, resulting in complex systems with poor conversion efficiency and overall low average and peak power. In this paper, we report on a watt-level dual-comb laser directly emitting at 2.1 $\mu$m. The system is based on a single-cavity, soft-aperture Kerr-lens mode-locked (KLM) laser using a broadband holmium (Ho)-doped CaAlGdO$_4$ (CALGO) gain crystal. The laser delivers a total output power exceeding 2 W (1 W per comb) with a sub-100-fs pulse duration (50 nm bandwidth) at a repetition rate of 96.5 MHz, corresponding to a pulse energy of 10 nJ and a peak power of 100 kW per comb. To assess the source's potential for future spectroscopic applications, we characterize the free-running dual comb in detail for frequency stability, phase noise, and relative intensity noise (RIN), and benchmark the achievable spectral resolution by measuring spectral modulations imposed by Fabry-P\'erot etalons. Our system combines the compactness, high efficiency, and passive mutual coherence of a single-cavity oscillator with watt-level average power at 2.1 $\mu$m, making it a promising source for environmental sensing in the atmospheric transmission window, or as a driver for nonlinear frequency conversion, for example, to the MIR and THz regions.

papers.title: Hierarchical universal open structure dataset for atomistic modeling
papers.summary: Atomic-scale simulations have been transformed by machine-learning models that predict the properties of atomistic structures with the accuracy of quantum calculations, but at a small fraction of the cost. These models have increased dramatically in generality, thanks to the availability of synthetic datasets of ever-increasing size and scope. The proliferation of datasets, with properties often computed using different levels of electronic-structure approximation, is problematic, as there is often overlap between different datasets, and strong correlations between structures obtained with short molecular dynamics trajectories or geometry optimization. To address these problems, we introduce a protocol to stratify a dataset into a hierarchy of nested subsets, subsampling from the coarsest to the finest resolution based on an "ecumetric" built to reflect the latent space representation of several popular universal machine-learning interatomic potentials. We then use this approach to combine most of the open structural datasets currently available, consolidating them into MAD-COSMO, a well-organized collection of almost 1.7 billion structures, whose $2^{24}$ most diverse members form the MAD-CORE stratified coreset, which can be easily used for all sorts of tasks, from exploratory experiments to the training of foundation models at scale. We envision that this collection will guide and help coordinate future efforts, focusing them on the most relevant and/or undersampled regions of chemical and structural space, and that it will be further extended to incorporate the outcomes of the collective work of this community.
