papers.title: Energetics of Fault-Tolerant Spin-Qubit Quantum Computation
papers.summary: Semiconductor spin qubits offer a promising route to compact and scalable quantum computers, combining long coherence times in isotopically purified silicon with compatibility with semiconductor manufacturing. Beyond computational speedup, their energy efficiency is an important consideration for future large-scale systems. We evaluate the power and energy requirements of a Loss-DiVincenzo spin-qubit quantum computer by analyzing the Quantum Fourier Transform (QFT) and benchmarking it against the classical Fast Fourier Transform (FFT). We develop a detailed energy budget, identifying cryogenic cooling as the dominant baseline contribution before quantum error correction (QEC). The comparison between the QFT and the classical FFT reveals that, for any quantum workload operating under a polynomially bounded sampling regime, the crossover in energy consumption occurs at smaller problem sizes than the crossover in execution time. Thus, quantum computing can become energetically competitive before achieving a speedup in execution time. We then incorporate surface-code QEC and analyze the energy costs of QEC cycles, gate synthesis, and decoding. At scale, instrumentation and decoding become dominant contributions, while cryogenic cooling imposes a constraint on scalability. We show that optimizing the control-signal demultiplexing ratio can reduce the overall energy cost by approximately two orders of magnitude. For a system with about one million physical qubits, we estimate a power consumption of approximately 100 kW, at least one order of magnitude below that of today's highest-performance classical computing systems.

papers.title: Efficient quantum simulation of unitary gates based on atomic ensembles
papers.summary: We develop a technique to perform efficient unitary time evolution of a general spin Hamiltonian based on the system with identical qubits, as naturally realized by permutation symmetric atomic ensembles. We employ Cartan decomposition method to the associated Hamiltonian Lie algebra and construct the symmetry adapted generators to implement unitary operator of the ensemble Hamiltonian. This enables the compact circuit representations of the system dynamics in terms of experimentally accessible collective spin operations and exploits the Dicke basis structure of the ensembles as an effective qudit representation. We benchmark Cartan based evolution against both exact time evolution and the Suzuki Trotter product formula. Our results show that the Cartan protocol accurately reproduces the operator dynamics, spin expectation values, and fluctuation observables with zero error that are substantially smaller than those obtained through Trotterization while maintaining an optimized circuit structure. In addition, scaling analysis with the ensemble size demonstrates that the Cartan error remains independent of the atom number while the corresponding Trotter error increases with the system size, highlighting the improved efficiency of the Cartan approach for a larger system size.

papers.title: Programmable all-to-all entangling gates for cavity-coupled atoms
papers.summary: Fault tolerant quantum computers greatly benefit from having both high fidelity entangling gates and a non-local qubit connectivity. However, most entangling gates for neutral atoms are local, requiring separated atoms to be moved using optical tweezers to yield entanglement between them. Here, we design a high fidelity M\o lmer S\o rensen-like entangling gate between neutral atoms coupled to a photonic cavity, enabling a programmable all-to-all connectivity through the shared cavity coupling. The gate is both robust to changes in cavity photon number, and enables selective entanglement between any subset of separated atoms through local laser addressing. This eliminates the need to physically move atoms to perform the gate, and therefore motional errors and erasure are suppressed. Using experimentally realistic parameters we demonstrate gate fidelities exceeding $F > 0.99$, with higher fidelities achievable through optimal control of the pump amplitudes.

papers.title: Constrained dissipation and the lifetime of quantum many-body scars
papers.summary: We investigate the fate of quantum many-body scars in the PXP model subject to Markovian dissipation. We show that when local jump operators respect the same symmetries of the Hamiltonian the full Liouvillian spectrum displays a tower of states with properties analogous to standard quantum scars: large overlaps with N\'eel states and equally spaced gaps in the imaginary part of the eigenvalues, set by a single frequency. Whether the long-time dynamics is dominated by scars is determined by the real parts of the eigenvalues, which are set by the ratio between the two relaxation rates $\gamma_{\pm}$ describing spin flips down-to-up or up-to-down respectively. For asymmetric dissipation ($\gamma_+ > \gamma_-$) the scarred eigenvalues have the smallest real parts: the resulting enhanced fidelity oscillations are further stabilized by staggered jump operators. In contrast, replacing the full projection operator in the dissipators with a partial one breaks the symmetries of the problem and is seen to destroy dissipative scars altogether.

papers.title: SynDebug: A Framework to Debug Logic Bugs in Fault-Tolerant Quantum Computing Programs
papers.summary: Fault-tolerant quantum computing (FTQC) introduces substantial systems-level complexity through quantum error correction (QEC), making debugging FTQC programs challenging. Existing quantum debugging approaches primarily target logical-level circuits and do not naturally support debugging within realistic FTQC execution flows. We present SynDebug, the first systems-level debugging framework for FTQC programs. SynDebug introduces lightweight assertion-based debugging primitives that operate directly within encoded FTQC infrastructures while avoiding additional logical surface area and minimizing temporal overhead. We evaluate SynDebug across multiple QEC code families, code distances, and encoded workloads, including state preparation, entanglement validation, and Shor-style programs. Our results demonstrate that SynDebug enables practical FTQC debugging with an average 1.8% additional circuit depth overhead (0% in most cases) and no measurable increase in the logical error rate, showing that systems-level debugging for large-scale FTQC applications is both feasible and practical.

papers.title: Classical Capacity of Single-Mode Bosonic Gaussian Channels
papers.summary: The classical capacity of a noisy optical channel is the maximum rate at which information can be transmitted reliably, given a constraint on the mean input energy. For the ubiquitous bosonic Gaussian channels, which include standard models of loss and noise in fibre and free-space optical links, determining this rate requires addressing whether entanglement between channel uses or non-Gaussian signals can outperform Gaussian encodings. More precisely, the question is whether the energy-constrained Holevo information is additive across arbitrarily many channel uses and coincides with its Gaussian counterpart. We answer these fundamental questions in the affirmative for every single-mode bosonic Gaussian channel at every input energy. Namely, we prove that independently prepared Gaussian states with Gaussian-distributed random displacements achieve the capacity, including in the low-energy regime where squeezing the signals competes with encoding information in their displacement. Our proof connects an entanglement inequality to a sharp, additive lower bound on output entropy. We then characterise communication above capacity: under a strict total photon-number cutoff, the probability of correct decoding decreases exponentially with the number of channel uses, and we derive explicit bounds on the decay exponent. When only the mean photon number is constrained, a simple energy-rescaling formula determines exactly the entire asymptotic rate--error trade-off: the capacity at mean photon number $N$ and allowed average decoding error $\epsilon$ equals the vanishing-error capacity at mean photon number $N/(1-\epsilon)$. Together, these results identify the ultimate limits of classical communication for some of the most fundamental models of optical communication.

papers.title: Magna: simulating magic state factories as cheaply as Clifford circuits
papers.summary: Classical simulation of magic state factories, including distillation, cultivation, and code switching, is challenging because of their substantial non-Clifford content. We introduce $\texttt{magna}$ (magic-state-factory assessment via global network algebra), a classical simulator that simulates such protocols as cheaply as Clifford circuits. $\texttt{magna}$ expresses the figures of merit of a protocol, namely the acceptance rate and the fidelity of the accepted states, as tensor networks, which it reduces globally by exploiting a structural correspondence with transversal gates on quantum codes. $\texttt{magna}$ further supports feedforward conditioned on arbitrary functions of mid-circuit measurement outcomes, including decoder outputs. We simulate Bravyi--Haah distillation with up to 100 output magic states at a cost that does not grow exponentially in the number of outputs, and achieve state-of-the-art sampling times for distance-5 magic state cultivation on both color codes and RP$^2$ surface codes. Finally, we validate nonlinear feedforward on a logical-level distillation protocol with 15 rounds of decoder-dependent feedforward. $\texttt{magna}$ aims to contribute to the key infrastructure for the large-scale evaluation and optimization of magic state factories.

papers.title: Magic in quantum trajectory unravelings of noisy random quantum circuits
papers.summary: The quantum-trajectory description of a noisy quantum circuit is not unique: every Kraus representation of the noise channel defines a different unraveling, i.e., a different ensemble of pure states that averages to the same density matrix. While all unravelings share the same expectation values of observables, they generally differ in the amount of quantum resources carried by the individual trajectories. Here we study non-stabilizerness, or magic, quantified by the stabilizer R\'enyi entropy, in quantum-trajectory unravelings of Haar-random and $T$-doped random Clifford brickwork circuits subject to local dephasing noise of strength $p$. The canonical unraveling in terms of Pauli jumps is Clifford and leaves magic untouched, so that trajectories retain the Haar-random value of non-stabilizerness. Exploring the full two-parameter family of minimal unravelings, we find that the trajectory-averaged magic can be substantially reduced by a state-independent choice of Kraus operators, and that the optimal choice is not in general the projective-measurement unraveling, but a two-outcome generalized measurement in which the Kraus operators correspond to a weak measurement of the noisy qubit. The optimal unraveling reduces the extensive magic density of the trajectories by a $p$-dependent factor without altering its linear scaling with system size. At the same time, it produces a very broad distribution of magic over trajectories, with a sizable fraction of trajectories retaining Haar-random magic. Since the cost of stabilizer-based classical simulation grows exponentially with the magic of the state, these high-magic trajectories, rather than the average, control the simulation cost. Our results delineate the potential and the limitations of unraveling optimization as a route to the classical simulation of noisy quantum dynamics with stabilizer methods.

papers.title: Stability of Quantum LDPC States under Local Pauli Noise
papers.summary: Quantum low-density parity-check (qLDPC) codes have a canonical mixed state---the normalized projector onto the code space---that lies at the intersection of quantum error correction and quantum many-body physics, yet the stability of its information-theoretic structure under local noise remains poorly understood. Recent progress on mixed-state phases of matter has identified the spatial decay of conditional mutual information (CMI) $I(A:C|B)$ as a key diagnostic of such stability, analogous to the role of the spectral gap for quantum ground states. We prove that, for the normalized code-projector state of a $\mathbb{Z}_d$ qLDPC stabilizer code under local Pauli noise, the CMI across a buffer $B$ separating $A$ from $C$ decays exponentially with the width of $B$ in two complementary noise regimes independent of system size. At weak noise, this holds for full-system tripartitions, where correlations between the two sides require an error cluster to cross the buffer, an exponentially unlikely event. At strong noise, exponential decay holds whenever the buffer supports no logical operator, since correlations can persist only along rare chains of buffer qudits that remain informative. Under an additional space-uniformity assumption, we establish the robustness of Levin--Wen topological entropy. On finite-dimensional lattices of size $n$, the weak-noise bound further implies a constant-layer quasi-local Petz recovery channel of range $O(\poly(\log n)/\varepsilon)$ that recovers the noiseless state within trace-distance error $\varepsilon$. Both CMI bounds apply to general qLDPC interaction graphs, including geometries where such constant-depth quasi-local recovery need not exist. Thus, the exponential decay of the noise-induced CMI provides a general criterion for mixed-state phase stability.

papers.title: Boundary-induced geometrical frustration in a square Rydberg-atom lattice
papers.summary: We study geometric defects in square-lattice Rydberg-atom arrays induced by lattice-size parity in the striated density-wave phase. While odd-sized lattices select a single striated domain, even-sized lattices seed incompatible domains at the four corners, resulting in a {\pi}/2-rotation invariant state with a geometrical defect emanating from the lattice center. At larger detunings, we instead identify a {\pi}-rotation-invariant state with two domains nucleated by opposite corners and separated by a one-dimensional diagonal defect. We probe the state-preparation protocol on the Aquila atomic quantum processor and benchmark it with equilibrium and real-time dynamics tensor-network simulations. Our results assess the role of boundaries and lattice size in determining the global ordering in programmable quantum matter.

papers.title: Long-lived local coherences at high temperature from frozen domain walls
papers.summary: Local coherences between distinct charge sectors--measured by the single-particle Green's function or the transverse spin autocorrelation function--do not overlap with hydrodynamic modes. At finite temperature, therefore, they decay faster than any power law in generic chaotic systems. We present a mechanism by which these coherences can persist anomalously long, for integrable and chaotic spin chains (including the XXZ and Fredkin spin chains) that obey a quantum group symmetry. We show--using a Mazur bound derived from the quantum-group symmetry, together with locality and a "non-undershoot" assumption--that the transverse spin autocorrelation function $C(t) \equiv \langle \sigma^-_x(t) \sigma^+_x(0)\rangle$ can decay at most algebraically: $C(t) \gtrsim 1/t^2$. This bound is not tight: in the large-anisotropy limit of the XXZ spin chain, at infinite temperature, we explicitly compute $C(t) \sim \sqrt{3}/(18 \sqrt{t})$. We also compute this decay rate in the XXZ spin chain for general easy-axis anisotropy, and estimate it to scale as $C(t) \sim t^{-2/z}$ (for transport exponent $z$) in the chaotic models.

papers.title: Localized states of the non-Hermitian Schr{\"o}dinger equation with a complex $1/r^{2}$ potential: from Efimov states to bipolarons
papers.summary: We study the non-Hermitian Schr\"odinger equation with a complex $1/r^{2}$ potential, which bridges Hermitian few-body and non-Hermitian many-body physics: a real attractive potential describes Efimov bound states, whereas a purely imaginary one describes the medium-induced interaction between two heavy polarons at large separations. We solve this equation analytically, obtaining both the localized and continuum states, and compare the solutions with numerical and WKB results. As the imaginary part of the potential is increased, the energies of the Efimov bound states acquire imaginary parts and rotate counterclockwise in the complex plane. On approaching the purely imaginary potential, the excited states disappear sequentially, while the Efimov ground state is smoothly connected to a bipolaron state localized at short distance. Such a bipolaron is localized solely by the medium-induced imaginary interaction, without any attractive real potential. Solving the equation by finite differences, we find that each bipolaron state is necessarily accompanied by another localized state that oscillates on the scale of the mesh size and hence has no counterpart in the continuum limit. Each such pair coalesces at an exceptional point as the strength of the purely imaginary potential is varied, whereas the coalescence is lifted once a finite real part is introduced. We show that this behavior originates from a symmetry of the discretized Schr\"odinger equation that holds for any purely imaginary potential.

papers.title: Finite-size geometric crossover toward fragmentation of the potential energy shell in the quantum random energy model
papers.summary: The quantum random energy model (QREM) is a paradigmatic model for studying delocalization-localization transitions at finite energy density in Fock space. In the computational basis, its diagonal energies are independent Gaussian random variables, in contrast to the correlated energies of local interacting models such as the disordered XXZ chain. In this work, we construct a potential energy shell associated with a basis state, defined through its energy variance, and investigate its connectivity on the Fock-space hypercube. As the transverse field is varied, this energy-selected subgraph undergoes a finite-size geometric crossover between fully connected and fragmented regimes. Furthermore, we observe a correlation between the shell connectivity and the finite-size fractal dimension of the eigenstates, as extracted from the participation entropy. For the QREM, the statistical independence of the diagonal energies allows the shell connectivity to be analyzed as an effective independent site percolation problem on the hypercube, with its crossover scale estimated within a one-hop approximation. At finite energy density, this estimate gives a nonmonotonic dependence of the crossover scale on system size $L$: increasing $L$ initially favors connectivity, while beyond an energy-dependent scale $L^*(\varepsilon)$ the trend reverses towards fragmentation.

papers.title: Theory of Dispersion and Exchange Interactions Subjected to Surface Roughness in Application to Signal Transmission through a Nanoswitch
papers.summary: We present the theoretical description of a resistive nanoswitch designated for a change-over between the two operation modes by calculating the electri elastic, dispersion (van der Waals and Casimir), and also exchange repulsive forces in its configuration with an account of surface roughness. The dispersion forces are described by means of the Lifshitz theory and, at the shortest separations between the interacting bodies, where this theory is inapplicable, by the method of additive summation of the interatomic potentials corrected for the role of the effects of nonadditivity. The exchange repulsion is also found by a summation of the interatomic potentials and using the proximity force approximation. It is shown that the nanoswitch possesses the equilibrium closest separation between a cantilever tip and a ground plate calculated as a function of the actuation voltage and operates in a cyclic manner with no pull-in when this voltage is switched on and off. We have found the tunnel current between a cantilever tip and a plate and investigated distortions appearing in the signal transmitted through a nanoswitch. According to our results, the amplitude distortions arising in the low-frequency information signal can be made sufficiently small by increasing a difference between the amplitudes of the carrier and information signals. Possible applications of the obtained results are discussed.

papers.title: Realization Divergence in Multi-Provider Quantum Computing: A Pre-Registered Study of What Survives Measurement
papers.summary: Quantum programs pass through compilers, transpilers and vendor services before execution. However, the distance between what was written and what runs is rarely measured. We call this distance realization divergence: the observable difference in how an identical source circuit is realized and behaves across quantum software stacks. We report a hardware study across three vendors and four devices, combining pre-registered predictions with explicitly identified exploratory analyses and amendments. In a compilation experiment with assigned placement policies, embedding radius correlates with two-qubit overhead at Spearman 0.805, against 0.492 for circuit size. Under a fixed lowest-index policy, an eight-qubit Bernstein-Vazirani circuit exhibits greater execution divergence than a twelve-qubit circuit on IQM Emerald. The opposite ordering occurs on IQM Garnet. Both comparisons replicate across two repetitions with disjoint confidence intervals. These results support a placement-dependent explanation, without isolating individual hardware noise mechanisms. The same ordering inversion is absent on the all-to-all IonQ control. On Rigetti Cepheus, a follow-up using topology-aware native placement found no consistent advantage in correct-answer probability for either submission track, but did not establish equivalence between the tracks. Structural comparisons depend on metric weighting, placement and device generation. Provider interfaces also limit observability: Rigetti's supported-operation list remained unchanged across a device generation that replaced the native entangler. We classify silent interface failures in composed toolchains and identify checks at toolchain boundaries, connecting valid cross-provider comparisons with concrete software-quality practices.

papers.title: Probing Deconfined Quantum Criticality Point on a Digital Quantum Computer
papers.summary: A deconfined quantum critical point (DQCP) is a continuous transition between ordered phases with unrelated broken symmetries, beyond the Landau-Ginzburg-Wilson paradigm. In one dimension, such a transition between a $z$-polarized ferromagnet (zFM) and a valence-bond solid (VBS) is well established numerically in a frustrated spin-$1/2$ chain. Here we ask whether a superconducting quantum processor can resolve this transition and its signatures despite finite-size effects and device noise. The ground states are prepared by ancilla-projected quantum imaginary-time evolution (QITE), whose exact target states are compressed by tensor-network optimization into shallow depth quantum circuits. The hardware data distinguish the phases through their order parameters, spin and dimer correlations, structure factors, correlation ratios, and snapshot distributions. The crossing of the order parameters locates the transition, and its finite-size extrapolation lies close to the thermodynamic-limit value obtained from large-scale numerics. A noise model based on the device calibration accounts quantitatively for the reduced amplitudes measured on hardware. Our findings demonstrate that a Landau-forbidden transition between competing orders can be resolved on current quantum processors.

papers.title: A complete classification of perfect state transfer in Grover walks on abelian Cayley graphs
papers.summary: We completely classify connected Cayley graphs over finite abelian groups that exhibit perfect state transfer in Grover walks. First, we show that a Cayley graph over any finite group exhibiting perfect state transfer has valency $1$, $2$, or $4$. For valency $4$, we prove that an abelian Cayley graph $\operatorname{Cay}(\Gamma,S)$ exhibits perfect state transfer if and only if $S=\{a,-a,a+h,-a+h\}$, where $h$ has order $2$, and $4\nmid |\Gamma|/2$. Combining this characterization with the valency-one and valency-two cases, we explicitly determine all pairs $(\Gamma,S)$ for which $\operatorname{Cay}(\Gamma,S)$ exhibits perfect state transfer. Our results extend the classification of circulant graphs of valency at most four obtained by Kubota and Yoshino [Circulant graphs with valency up to 4 that admit perfect state transfer in Grover walks, \emph{J. Comb. Theory Ser. A.}, 216 (2025) 106064] to Cayley graphs over arbitrary finite abelian groups and to all valencies.

papers.title: Classification of bipartite observables III: simplicity, mixtures and quantum error correction
papers.summary: The paradigm of a simple unstable theory in the sense of Shelah is the theory of the random graph, the Fra\"iss\'e limit of the finite graphs. Quantum error correction has a paradigm of its own, and we show that it is the counterpart of the random graph: the Pauli group on countably many qubits, taken modulo phases and with commutation as its relation, is the Fra\"iss\'e limit of the finite alternating spaces over the two-element field, and its form computes the syndromes of stabilizer codes. Seen through this correspondence, simplicity theory turns out to be a theory of error correction. Clifford encoding circuits implement the homogeneity of the Pauli group, forking recognizes the logical errors, and the independence theorem of Kim and Pillay is the gluing of syndromes. The two paradigms look alike as first-order structures, and they part company only when observables enter. Each defines a bipartite observable, and we prove that, once preparations are mixed, both acquire the tree property of the second kind in real-valued logic. They reach it by different roads, however, and we show that the probes decide which. The probes of the Pauli observable are the Pauli channels; for them the indicator of each syndrome sector is the difference of the responses of two uniform mixtures, and actual mixtures already witness the tree. The probes of the Rado observable see only marginals; conditions given by actual mixtures remain compatible on disjoint blocks, and the tree must be sought among idealized preparations.

papers.title: Quantum Systems as results of Geometric Evolutions
papers.summary: In the framework of deterministic finslerian models, a mechanism producing dissipative dynamics at the Planck scale is discussed. It is based on a geometric evolution from Finsler to Riemann structures defined on the fiber bundle ${ TM}\to { M}$. Quantum states are equivalence classes, composed by the configurations that evolve through an internal dynamics drive by the above geometric evolution. Each equivalence class is conformed by the ontological states that evolve to the same final state. The existence of an hermitian scalar product in an associated linear space is discussed and related with the quantum pre-Hilbert space. This hermitian product emerges from geometric and statistical considerations. Our scheme recovers the main ingredients of the usual Quantum Mechanics. Several consequences are discussed and compared with the predictions of the standard Quantum Mechanics. A natural solution of the cosmological constant problems is proposed, as well as a mechanism for the absence of quantum interferences at classical scales.

papers.title: Imposing Constraints on Driver Hamiltonians and Mixing Operators: From Theory to Practical Implementation
papers.summary: Driver Hamiltonians and Mixing Operators that satisfy constraints is an important part of ansatz construction for many quantum algorithms. In this manuscript, we give general algebraic expressions for finding Hamiltonian terms and analogously unitary primitives, that satisfy constraint embeddings and use these to give complexity characterizations of the related problems. We prove that knowing if operators exist that enforce classical constraints is NP-Complete in the general case, but give algorithmic procedures with worse-case polynomial runtime to find any operators with a constant locality bound; a useful result since many constraints imposed admit local operators to enforce them in practice. We then give algorithmic procedures to turn these algebraic primitives into Hamiltonian drivers and unitary mixers that can be used for Constrained Quantum Annealing (CQA) and Quantum Alternating Operator Ansatz (QAOA) constructions by tackling practical problems related to finding an appropriate set of reduced generators and defining corresponding drivers and mixers accordingly. We consider a new QAOA approach based on the maximally disjoint subset as well as higher order constraint satisfaction terms for 1-in-3 SAT, which dramatically outperform the X-mixer.

papers.title: Low-overhead tailoring and learning of noise in graph states
papers.summary: Graph and hypergraph states are important resource states for realizing universal quantum computation and diverse non-local physical phenomena. However, noise learning in such states is challenging due to their large entanglement and magic. This work establishes a low Clifford hierarchy circuit-based scheme for tailoring and learning noise in (hyper)graph states generated by multiple controlled-Z gates. The key is to convert the noisy input state into diagonal form and derive the convolution equation for the diagonal noise rates, which has a lower resource overhead. Such a diagonal form can be used in real quantum simulation by using the same conversion technique on the graph state input. We demonstrate that a single-depth Bell measurement is sufficient in our scheme for arbitrary graph states, while noise tailoring can be done via Pauli operations. After that, we suggest the Walsh-Hadamard transform and some approximation method for decoding the convolution equation to estimate the tailored noise. We prove that constant sampling and polynomial time complexities are sufficient to guarantee bounded noise estimation error with respect to the $l_2$-norm, which usually requires exponential complexity with existing noise estimation methods. The polynomial complexities are maintained even for the more stringent $l_1$ approximation under the sparse noise assumption. Conclusively, we propose novel methods for characterizing the noise properties of an entangled state at a lower cost than that of state generation. Moreover, compared with state verification methods, we can attain richer information on noise rates and enable noise mitigation, thereby providing guarantees for the preparation of graph states.

papers.title: Entanglement Detection with Rotationally Covariant Measurements -- From Compton Scattering to Lemonade
papers.summary: The accurate and efficient detection of quantum entanglement remains a central challenge in quantum information science. In this work, we study the detection of entanglement of polarized photons for measurement devices that are specified by rotational covariance. We derive explicit positive operator-valued measures (POVMs) showing that any such (idealized) setting is classified by one real measurable parameter r. In particular, we give a POVM formulation of the Klein-Nishina formula for Compton scattering of polarized photons. We provide an SDP-based entanglement certification method with computable bounds that operates on the full measured statistics, also considering semi-device independent scenarios. Furthermore, we show that, while Bell violations are impossible with two rotationally covariant measurements, EPR steering can still be certified under one-sided symmetry constraints. Finally, we demonstrate how our approach can be applied by analyzing a rotationally covariant showcase experiment using scattered polarized light in a selection of soft drinks. Our results motivate further investigation of entanglement detection with lemonade- based detectors.

papers.title: General Quantum Protocol for Communication via $n$--Qubit GHZ States
papers.summary: This study presents a generalized $n$--bit superdense coding protocol that enables the transmission of n classical bits of information using an entangled $n$--qubit quantum system and the transmission of $n-1$ qubits. The protocol involves creating a maximally entangled $n$--qubit GHZ state, encoding the classical message with Pauli--Z and Pauli--X gates, and then transmitting and decoding the message via quantum communication, quantum operations, and measurements. The key novelty of this work is an explicit, scalable $n$--bit encoding routine, realized on the GHZ channel with a low--depth encoding layer using only single--qubit Pauli--X and Pauli--Z operations. The protocol was tested on real quantum hardware using Qiskit 2.0 and the IBM--Fez quantum computer for message lengths of 4, 6, 8, and 10 bits, as a circuit--level proof of concept on a single processor; the physical transmission of qubits between the parties was not implemented. Results show that success rates decrease as message length, transpiled circuit depth and gate count increase; the latter two are set mainly by transpilation rather than by the encoding itself. A mutual information analysis shows that the transmitted information exceeds the classical bound of $n-1$ bits only for short messages. Strategies to improve performance include sending messages in shorter segments and advances in qubit coherence and gate fidelity. This work offers a practical and easily scalable quantum communication protocol with potential applications in quantum networks and communication systems.

papers.title: Heisenberg-limited metrology from the quantum-quench dynamics of an anisotropic ferromagnet
papers.summary: The emerging field of quantum magnonics seeks to understand and harness the quantum properties of magnons -- quantized collective spin excitations in magnets. Squeezed magnon states arise naturally as the equilibrium ground states of anisotropic ferromagnets and antiferromagnets, representing an important class of nonclassical magnon states. In this work, we show how a qubit-conditioned quantum quench of an anisotropic ferromagnet can be used for Heisenberg-limited parameter estimation based on measurements of the qubit only. In the presence of ground-state squeezing, the protocol yields information about the eigenmode frequency of the coupled magnon-qubit system, whereas no information is gained in the absence of such squeezing. The protocol therefore leverages genuine quantum correlations in the form of magnonic squeezing while simultaneously relying on the equilibrium character of this squeezing -- a feature distinctive to magnetic systems.

papers.title: Thermodynamics of linear open quantum walks
papers.summary: Open quantum systems interact with their environment, leading to nonunitary dynamics. We investigate the thermodynamics of linear Open Quantum Walks (OQWs), a class of quantum walks whose dynamics is entirely driven by the environment. We define an equilibrium temperature, identify a population inversion near a finite critical value of a control parameter, analyze the thermalization process, and develop the statistical mechanics needed to describe the thermodynamical properties of linear OQWs. We also study nonequilibrium thermodynamics by analyzing the time evolution of entropy, energy, and temperature, while providing analytical tools to understand the system's evolution as it converges to the thermalized state. We examine the validity of the second and third laws of thermodynamics in this setting. Finally, we employ these developments to shed light on dissipative quantum computation within the OQW framework.

papers.title: Geometric Optimization over Quantum State Spaces: Tight Uncertainty Relations and Resource Certification
papers.summary: Determining the fundamental limits of nonlinear functionals of quantum measurement statistics is a crucial yet generally intractable nonconvex optimization problem. We introduce a generic support-function-based outer-approximation framework for solving concave-minimization (or convex-maximization) problems over the quantum state space. By mapping the problem onto a reduced $\mathcal{Z}$ space, we characterize the exact quantum boundary through supporting half space derived from the largest eigenvalues of effective observables. This yields an effective method that produces tight bounds for general measurements in finite-dimensional quantum systems with preassigned numerical precision. As an initial application, we recover the exact variance-based uncertainty relations of [PRL \textbf{119}, 170404 (2017)] and efficiently compute optimal entropic uncertainty relations (EURs). Our results reveal that standard analytical and majorization-based EUR bounds are fundamentally loose for generic measurements, and we show that the resulting exact bounds directly enhance quantum steering detection under asymmetric settings. We further apply the framework to determine the maximal athermality resource certifiable from a restricted measurement scenario. Our method thus provides a universal computational tool for exploring the boundaries of quantum state space and the limits of quantum resources.

papers.title: Contractivity of time-dependent driven-dissipative systems
papers.summary: Experimentally relevant quantum systems are frequently described by a time-dependent Lindblad master equation in which the dissipation due to interaction with an environment is fixed, but the experimenter has control over the Hamiltonian, which therefore can change with time. A fundamental question that is also of practical relevance is to determine when such systems invariably lose information about their initial state (are exponentially contractive independent of the Hamiltonian) or when the control can be used to prevent this loss of information to some degree. Here, we identify the necessary and sufficient criterion on the dissipator for Hamiltonian-invariant contractivity. If the dissipator does not fulfil this criterion, but by itself is exponentially contractive, we also establish exponential contractivity for sufficiently weak or slow drives and construct examples where strong or fast driving prevents exponential contraction.

papers.title: Obstacles to Continuous Quantum Error Correction via Parity Measurements
papers.summary: Time-continuous quantum error correction, necessary to protect quantum information under time-dependent Hamiltonians, relies on weak continuous syndrome measurements. Implementing these measurements requires a continuous coupling among at least two qubits and a meter, a demanding requirement. We show that, under continuous operation, common parity-measurement protocols in the circuit quantum electrodynamics platform corrupt the logical information. The failure arises from approximating the three-body interaction by a sum of two-body couplings to the meter, which prevents simultaneous suppression of measurement backaction on the logical and error subspaces. We argue that the same mechanism applies more generally beyond the circuit quantum electrodynamics setting. Taken together, our results impose a practical limitation on continuous stabilizer quantum error correction and point to the viable alternatives -- architectures that realize native three-body interactions, or erasure-based encodings in which the error subspace need not be protected.

papers.title: Implementation of non-local arbitrary two-qubit controlled gates via geometric quantum computation with Rydberg anti-blockade
papers.summary: In the context of Rydberg anti-blockade, this paper proposes a new scheme for a high-fidelity controlled-unitary gate based on non-adiabatic holonomic quantum computation. Under specific detuning and interaction conditions, the scheme achieves a suitable evolution path for non-adiabatic holonomic quantum computation through reverse engineering of pulse parameters. This scheme can implement arbitrary two-qubit controlled gates with favorable robustness. We also evaluate the effects of spontaneous emission and laser intensity errors on the fidelity; numerical simulations show that the geometric gate scheme still exhibits excellent performance under these errors. Furthermore, we extend the scheme to non-local gates via entanglement transfer and quantum teleportation techniques, and demonstrate its application in the mutual conversion among four-qubit entangled states (GHZ, cluster, and W states). This finding indicates the potential applicability of our scheme to complex quantum information processing tasks.

papers.title: Instability-enhanced quantum sensing with tunable multibody interactions
papers.summary: Dynamical instabilities can amplify small perturbations into measurable signals, offering a route to quantum-enhanced sensing. This mechanism was experimentally demonstrated in a collective spin system with quadratic interactions, described by a twist-and-turn Hamiltonian, where quantum evolution near an unstable point leads to exponential growth of spin fluctuations, enabling metrological gain beyond the standard quantum limit. Here, we show that a quartic extension of this Hamiltonian substantially increases the amplification. This additional nonlinear term reshapes the phase-space structure, generating new unstable fixed points with larger local Lyapunov exponents and therefore faster signal amplification at shorter evolution times. Remarkably, even for the same instability rate (equal Lyapunov exponent), collective multibody interactions outperform the quadratic case, demonstrating that metrological gain is not determined by the Lyapunov exponent alone. We show analytically that the finite-time growth of the gain is governed also by the local phase-space curvature around the unstable point. Only for a symmetric unstable point, as in the quadratic case, is the finite-time gain described by the Lyapunov exponent alone. Our results identify local phase-space curvature as an additional resource for optimizing the speed and performance of quantum sensors.

papers.title: Clock-transition-enabled long electron spin coherence of telecom emitters in CeO$_2$
papers.summary: Rare-earth-ion-doped crystals has emerged as a promising platform for quantum technologies, owing to their narrow telecom-band optical emission, long spin memory, and compatibility with silicon integrated photonic architectures. However, the realization of scalable quantum devices requires host materials with intrinsically dilute spin environments to suppress decoherence. In this context, erbium (Er$^{3+}$) doped cerium oxide (CeO$_2$) is an attractive candidate due to the ultra-low concentration of nuclear spins in the host matrix and its compatibility with silicon-based technologies. Here we perform a comprehensive investigation of the coherence properties of Er$^{3+}$ electron spin qubit in CeO$_2$ via semiclassical as well as detailed cluster correlation expansion simulations. By systematically exploring magnetic field strength, pulse sequences, erbium concentration, and spin temperature, we identify regimes where decoherence from the spin bath is strongly suppressed. Our investigations illustrate that at dilute doping concentration (of the order of 10 ppb) and sub-Kelvin temperatures, operation near clock transitions enables Hahn-echo coherence times to approach the second timescale even at natural isotopic abundance. Importantly, from a practical standpoint, coherence times on the order of $\sim 10$ ms are expected even at liquid helium temperature (about 2 K) for similar concentrations. Moreover, we demonstrate that an additional enhancement can be obtained with conventional multi-$\pi$-pulse dynamical decoupling protocols. Thus, our findings establish Er$^{3+}$ doped CeO$_2$ as a front-runner for realizing spin qubits, quantum memories, and integrated quantum networks.

papers.title: The bulk spectral gap is certifiable from above but uncomputable from below
papers.summary: Determining spectral gaps in the thermodynamic limit is a central challenge in quantum many-body physics. When a fixed boundary condition is imposed, this problem is undecidable: no algorithm, even with unlimited resources, can decide for every Hamiltonian whether it is gapped. Yet the thermodynamic limit is meant to capture the intrinsic properties of very large systems, which should not depend on how their boundaries are chosen. Here, we therefore consider the bulk spectral gap problem, which concerns only the intrinsic excitations of the infinite system, independently of any boundary. We first give a general algorithm producing a hierarchy of certified upper bounds on the bulk gap, arbitrarily tight at the cost of more computation. Second, we prove that the spectral gap problem remains undecidable in the bulk: no algorithm can decide whether the bulk gap is positive, already for translationally invariant nearest-neighbour chains of fixed local dimension. The bulk spectral gap is thus certifiable from above but uncomputable from below. More precisely, the bulk-gaplessness promise problem is RE-complete, exactly as hard as the halting problem. The same construction also shows that deciding whether an explicitly given state is a ground state of the infinite system is undecidable. Finally, we apply the upper-bounding algorithm to the spin-1/2 kagome Heisenberg antiferromagnet to produce the first nontrivial certified upper bounds on its bulk gap.

papers.title: Optimal Calibration of Quantum Network Links
papers.summary: The reliable distribution of entanglement is essential for the effective operation of quantum networks. Due to fundamental differences between quantum and classical communication systems, it is necessary to develop specialised algorithms and protocols that also account for quantum-specific constraints. In this work, we focus on the issue of recalibration. As suggested by recent experimental studies, the process of local entanglement generation in a quantum link degrades over time due to environmental changes that have to be estimated and compensated via a fixed-duration calibration operation, during which the link is not available. Therefore, in such a quantum network, every link alternates between an activation period, during which it operates normally, and a calibration period, during which it cannot participate in the end-to-end entanglement distribution, thereby creating a trade-off between link quality (the initial fidelity of generated pairs, which decays during activation) and availability (the fraction of time the link is usable, which calibration reduces). We develop analytically a protocol for optimally assigning activation periods to each link in linear quantum repeater chains, subject to any general end-to-end fidelity requirements and local initial fidelity thresholds. Building on this foundation, we extend to general quantum networks, where multiple paths may cross at common links. To this, we propose a heuristic approach, evaluate it through simulations, and compare its performance with a benchmark, a numerical approach and theoretical bounds, confirming the analytical ordering of their performance.

papers.title: Quantum steering in networks: Measurement-device-independent detection, continuous variables, and practical Gaussian schemes
papers.summary: We consider quantum steering certification in multipartite networks, with a focus on minimal trust scenarios: all-except-one parties are untrusted and treated device-independently. We show that it is always possible to lift steering certification to the measurement-device-independent regime, in which even the (last) trusted party can treat their local hardware as a black-box, except for a set of fiduciary quantum states used as the inputs to the experiment. This holds both for finite-dimensional systems as well as for bosonic continuous-variable systems, which we characterize in terms of semi-quantum games in the bipartite case. Additionally, we introduce measurement-device-independent network steering protocols based entirely on Gaussian operations -- which cannot be used for fully device-independent protocols, and thus become instead a viable option for minimal trust certification as soon as a single trusted input is inserted in the network. Our results present a basis for steering-based applications (such as randomness generation) with minimal trust beyond full nonlocality and with feasible experimental requirements.

papers.title: Calculating strongly correlated ground states from the non-Markovian dissipative dynamics of Gaussian fermions
papers.summary: We introduce a mapping between the ground state of interacting fermionic Hamiltonians and the non-equilibrium steady state of a purely dissipative open quantum system. Within the framework of third quantization, we map the Fermi-Hubbard Hamiltonian onto Lindblad jump operators acting on Majorana fermions. Remarkably, both hopping and interaction terms map onto jump operators that preserve the Gaussianity of Majorana fermions along individual quantum trajectories. As a result, the dynamics can be unravelled and each trajectory can be simulated efficiently using only two-point correlation functions, with a computational cost that scales polynomially with system size. We further show that finite particle number requires negative dissipative rates, leading to an intrinsically non-Markovian dynamics. The corresponding trajectory unravelling involves both positive and negative stochastic weights and exhibits a sign problem and large fluctuations, so that convergence requires an exponentially large number of trajectories. The overall computational cost remains exponential in system size despite the efficient Gaussian representation of individual trajectories, but is crucially dependent on the computational complexity of the non-Markovian unravelling, motivating further studies on the efficiency of such unravellings.

papers.title: Sparse anisotropic positive maps for qutrit entanglement: exact indecomposability and PPT geometry
papers.summary: Positive but not completely positive maps provide one of the most direct ways to detect entanglement beyond the positive-partial-transpose (PPT) criterion. We introduce and analyze an exactly solvable two-parameter family of sparse bistochastic positive maps on qutrits, in which two coherence channels are independently tuned by parameters $w$ and $z$. The sparse structure makes the full phase diagram analytic: positivity holds exactly on the square $0\le w,z\le2/3$, complete positivity on the smaller square $0\le w,z\le1/3$, and decomposability is lost precisely outside a quarter circle in the corner $w,z\ge1/3$. The indecomposable region is certified by explicit PPT entangled state adapted to the same witness geometry. At the endpoint $W_*=W(2/3,2/3)$ we construct a four-parameter family of PPT edge states of rank type $(5,5)$, derive their analytic detection region, and show that the corresponding rays are exposed faces of the PPT cone. Finally, although $W_*$ is not optimal, we give an explicit optimal refinement whose detection region on this family is strictly larger. The result is an analytically tractable qutrit setting in which positivity, indecomposability, PPT entanglement, optimality, and exposed convex geometry can be studied in a single framework.

papers.title: Coherent-State Kernels for Composite Quantum Operations
papers.summary: This paper develops a unified kernel-based method for computing exact matrix elements of composite quantum operations by inserting resolutions of the identity after individual operators or between successive factors of an operator chain. A single insertion gives an exact scalar identity, and nested insertions between the factors give multiple integral identities for chains of closed operators under explicit Bochner-integrability conditions. The procedure is carried through on polynomial and analytic functions of the ladder operators, on one- and two-mode Gaussian unitaries, and on three composite operations: a Kerr phase followed by squeezing or by a cubic phase gate, a two-mode squeezer followed by a beam splitter, and a heralded cat-state circuit with two beam splitters. At rational Kerr phases the Kerr-squeezed amplitudes reduce to finite sums of squeezed coherent-state amplitudes weighted by quadratic Gauss sums, with an explicit error bound at the remaining phases; the two-mode network gives a bivariate Hermite polynomial; and the heralded circuit gives closed forms for the amplitudes, the heralding probabilities and their extension to an arbitrary passive network fed by one squeezed source. The examples are set against the reach of four established techniques: operator ordering, the Berezin symbol calculus, Lie disentangling and the symplectic formalism. Each technique reaches a subset of the examples directly, while the insertion procedure reaches all of them under the same hypotheses. A comparison with direct Fock summation identifies the regime in which the finite Kerr sums are efficient, and the choice of resolution at each boundary of a chain follows a selection rule set by the action of the adjacent factor. Each closed form agrees with an independent numerical computation.

papers.title: Phase Retrievability of Super Operators and Measurements
papers.summary: We continue the study of Phase Retrieval in the Quantum Information setting in the style of \cite{liu2023phase}, in a manner which is more general in two primary ways: (a) Instead of only pure states we consider also states (and positive semidefinite operators) of bounded rank, as is done in Quantum Tomography; (b) We consider general super operators instead of only quantum channels. We show that in order to have phase retrieval with respect to positive semidefinite operators of bounded rank, it suffices to discriminate between perfectly distinguishable pairs (i.e. those with orthogonal supports). From this we prove that phase retrievability is always Lipschitz stable with respect to the trace norm, and then we use the Fuchs-van de Graaf inequalities to deduce stability with respect to the Bures--Wasserstein distance (thus generalizing the known stability results for phase retrieval in Frame Theory). For Hermitian-preserving super operators taking values in block-diagonal matrices, we characterize phase retrievability in terms of conditions inspired by the classical complement property from Frame Theory.

papers.title: Parity-Based Time-Bin Encoding Enabling SWAP Between Polarization and Time-Bin Qubits
papers.summary: Multi-degree-of-freedom photonic quantum processing requires routing between degree-of-freedom (DOF) qubit encodings on a single photon. A SWAP between polarization and time-bin qubits is an advantageous primitive for such architectures, however conventional early/late time-bin encoding does not support bidirectional logical time-bin flips from late to early which limits the ability to implement certain quantum operations. We introduce a parity-based time-bin encoding in which logical $\ket{0}_T$ and $\ket{1}_T$ correspond to even and odd multiples of a spacing $\Delta t$, so that a physical delay of $\Delta t$ implements $\ket{0}_T \leftrightarrow \ket{1}_T$. This encoding is the enabling ingredient that makes a polarization-controlled delay line implement $\mathrm{CNOT}_{P \rightarrow T}$ and aligns naturally with periodic refractive index modulation for $\mathrm{CNOT}_{T \rightarrow P}$. Composing three such CNOT operations sequentially results in a deterministic SWAP between polarization and time-bin degrees of freedom. We quantify how EOM voltage errors reduce the polarization-flip probability and estimate timing requirements from modulator switching, detector resolution, and timing jitter, giving an illustrative timing budget.

papers.title: Optimality of Gaussian Entanglement of Formation
papers.summary: We prove that the entanglement of formation of every two-mode Gaussian state coincides with its Gaussian restriction, solving a longstanding open problem in continuous variable quantum information theory. The key result is a sharp affine relation between entanglement and a generalized Einstein--Podolsky--Rosen observable, valid for arbitrary pure two-mode states, including non-Gaussian ones. We further prove that the entanglement of formation is additive on arbitrary tensor products of two-mode Gaussian states, and hence coincides with the entanglement cost, settling the latter for all two-mode Gaussian states. As a consequence, we obtain in closed form the entanglement cost of thermal-loss, thermal-amplifier and additive-noise bosonic channels. Our results, which also extend to bisymmetric multimode states, establish that no two-mode state is less entangled than the Gaussian state with the same covariance matrix, yielding measurable lower bounds on both the entanglement of formation and the entanglement cost of arbitrary non-Gaussian states.

papers.title: Error Correction in a Distributed Quantum Computer
papers.summary: Building fault-tolerant quantum computers with large numbers of logical qubits requires both scalable hardware architectures and error-correcting codes that make efficient use of physical qubits. Photonic interconnects address both of these challenges by allowing the physical qubits to be distributed across multiple processors while providing the non-local connectivity necessary to implement resource-efficient codes such as high-rate quantum low-density parity-check (qLDPC) codes. A key requirement for realising this architecture is the ability to perform stabiliser measurements between remote processors, which has not previously been demonstrated experimentally. Here we report the first experimental demonstration of distributed quantum error detection and correction. We generate entanglement between network qubits in two separate trapped-ion processors and use it to perform remote syndrome measurements on data qubits. We first realise a distributed [[2, 1, 1]] repetition code, detecting phase-flip errors on a logical qubit encoded across the two modules in real time and suppressing logical errors. We then combine these mid-circuit syndrome measurements with real-time feedforward to actively correct arbitrary single-qubit Pauli errors on a distributed Bell state. These results provide an experimental foundation for quantum error correction (QEC) across modular quantum architectures.

papers.title: Quantum computational advantage in random-circuit sampling on IBM superconducting quantum computers
papers.summary: We report forward random-circuit sampling (RCS) on the 120-qubit Nighthawk r2 superconducting processor (ibm_phoenix) with square-lattice connectivity, using 61 qubits, native CZ gates, and the standard cloud execution stack with no benchmark-specific calibration. Two independent fidelity estimators---mirror benchmarking and three- and four-patch cross-entropy benchmarking (XEB)---agree with each other at every measured depth, the mirror from 4 to 40 cycles and the patched estimators from 20 to 40 cycles, across more than two orders of magnitude of fidelity decay, and exceed the first-generation Nighthawk r1 device by more than an order of magnitude at fixed depth. The 36-cycle circuits sit at the depth where tensor-network contraction cost saturates at system size: a contraction-cost estimator validated against the published Sycamore and Zuchongzhi networks places the single-amplitude cost at $\sim$$10^{22}$ complex operations. At $F_{\mathrm{XEB}}(36)=2.3\times10^{-3}$ under favorable memory assumptions this implies $1.2\times10^{27}$ machine operations within the bounded-fidelity rejection-sampling model --- more than a century of runtime on the Frontier supercomputer --- to collect a $10^{6}$-sample ensemble, which takes only 19\,s on Nighthawk r2. To our knowledge, this is the first demonstration of quantum advantage for a vanilla random-circuit sampling on a commercially and broadly accessible quantum processor that most non-expert quantum computer users can easily replicate.

papers.title: Quantum Uncertainty and Particle Trajectories: From Heisenberg and Schr\"odinger to Constructive Dynamical Models
papers.summary: Quantum uncertainty emerged from two strikingly different routes to quantum mechanics. Heisenberg's matrix mechanics replaced the classical description of atomic orbits by relations among observable transition quantities and led, in 1927, to the uncertainty relation and its influential measurement-based interpretation. Schr\"odinger's wave mechanics grew instead from the Bose--Einstein and de Broglie developments and restored a continuous space-time description through matter waves. The two formalisms were soon shown to be closely related, but neither historical route by itself settles the ontological question of whether particles may possess underlying trajectories. After reviewing these developments, including Einstein's criticism of a simple observability doctrine and Mott's wave-mechanical account of straight cloud-chamber tracks, we distinguish precise quantum uncertainty relations from the stronger claim that quantum mechanics excludes definite microscopic histories. We then compare Feynman paths, Bohmian trajectories, Nelson's stochastic mechanics, and finite-speed persistent Goldstein--Kac dynamics. The Kac process has continuous, piecewise differentiable finite-speed paths; its diffusion limit approaches Wiener kinematics, while analytic continuation of its two-sector dynamics is related to Dirac evolution. These examples show that quantum uncertainty relations constrain observable statistics without, by themselves, uniquely determining an underlying path geometry.

papers.title: Separability rigidity of Gaussian states under positive domination
papers.summary: We prove a separability rigidity theorem for finite-mode Gaussian states. Let $\rho_G$ be Gaussian and let $\mathcal I$ be a fixed partition of the modes. If $\rho_G$ dominates a nonzero positive operator $T$ that is separable across $\mathcal I$, $0\neq T\preccurlyeq \rho_G$, then $\rho_G$ itself is separable across $\mathcal I$. The dominated operator is arbitrary and need not be Gaussian. The theorem has three applications. First, any Gaussian channel admitting a nonzero entanglement-breaking completely positive subchannel is itself entanglement breaking, even when that subchannel is non-Gaussian. Second, if a resource state dominates a positive multiple of a faithful separable state, no finite-copy, postselected separability-preserving protocol can prepare an entangled Gaussian state exactly with nonzero success probability. Third, a connected graph of entangled Gaussian two-mode marginals certifies genuine multipartite entanglement of every compatible global state, even if the global state is non-Gaussian; the certification is robust to sufficiently small trace-norm errors in the marginals. As a structural corollary, mixing states separable across different partitions cannot produce new Gaussian states, so full inseparability and genuine multipartite entanglement coincide for finite-mode Gaussian states and identical copies of a biseparable Gaussian state cannot activate genuine multipartite entanglement.

papers.title: Robustness of quantum spectrum estimation: weak Schur sampling under noisy inputs
papers.summary: We initiate the study of weak Schur sampling (WSS) under noisy inputs. Many optimal quantum learning algorithms rely on this measurement, for instance in quantum spectrum estimation (QSE) and quantum state tomography (QST). The standard analysis of WSS, QSE and QST assumes that the $n$ input copies of the target state $\rho$ are identical, i.e. $\rho^{\otimes n}$. We study what happens when they are not, a more realistic noisy scenario that breaks the very permutation symmetry on which WSS is built. In the simplest model the input is a noisy product state: the copies are independent but not necessarily identical and each is $\epsilon$-close in trace distance to the $d$-dimensional target state $\rho$. A naive argument via the data-processing inequality allows the per-copy errors to accumulate to $n\epsilon$ on the measurement outcome. We show that for QSE via WSS this does not happen: the expected estimation error in total variation is at most $\epsilon+\eta(n,d)$, where $\eta(n,d)=O(d/\sqrt n)$ is the noiseless error, and the additive noise term $\epsilon$ is optimal. The output error does not grow with $n$ even though the input error does; in this sense WSS is robust. Beyond noisy product states, for arbitrary input $\omega$ we show that the error is at most $\eta(n,d)+\frac{1}{n}\|\omega-\rho^{\otimes n}\|_{W_1}$, where $W_1$ is the quantum Wasserstein distance of De Palma et al. In particular, our results imply, for the first time, noise-robustness of Keyl and Werner's seminal algorithm for QSE, more than two decades after its introduction. Finally, we show that the noise cannot be too bad: within our model of robustness the promise on the input cannot be weakened to closeness of single-copy marginals or to a global trace-distance budget alone, as in both cases some inputs defeat every measurement and estimator.

papers.title: Exact distances and measurement allocation for logical Pauli readout
papers.summary: The minimum fault weight of a logical readout depends jointly on data-error persistence, check redundancy and time-boundary constraints. For any binary check matrix $H$ and nonzero parity support $w$, we prove that a repeated-readout model with a zero-syndrome endpoint has exact distance $\min_{w\cdot y=1}[\operatorname{wt}(y)+q\operatorname{wt}(Hy)]$ for at least $q$ wrong readouts. This reduces the search over fault histories to one weighted spatial minimum and gives the minimum repetition count for each adjacent-column check in square Bacon--Shor and generalized Shor readouts. Combining those checks with redundant Gauss-check pair products yields an exact joint distance and an outcome-count optimum within the specified gauged-readout family. At target distance $m$, one round uses $m^2$ outcomes, compared with $m(2m-1)$ for the repeated baseline in the same phenomenological model. For a one-epoch bare-ancilla CNOT implementation, we prove a schedule-dependent distance upper bound by constructing an accepted wrong readout from one gate fault and outcome flips. The bound identifies necessary timing conditions for retaining the target distance and gives matching upper bounds of three for the best tested schedules at both $m=3$ and $m=5$.

papers.title: Efficient Learning of Structured Fermionic States under General Quadratic Evolution
papers.summary: We prove copy-optimal learning of the full Gaussian orbit of paired magic states on $n$ fermionic modes. The unknown evolution may be any parity-preserving quadratic circuit, including pair creation and annihilation, and each copy is measured once, in a fixed basis, on a single quartic Majorana observable. A nonadaptive learner returns a Gaussian preparation within trace distance $\epsilon$ from $\Theta(n^6/\epsilon^2)$ copies at fixed confidence, and no learner in this measurement model, adaptive or not, can do better. Measured quartic correlations certify the trace distance of the result. Our second result extends learning to a broader family: pure states whose unknown input blocks are superpositions of disjoint occupation patterns with bounded particle number, under the same evolution. Using single-copy Gaussian rotations and occupation readout, a batch-adaptive learner returns an input and a Gaussian circuit with infidelity $f$ from $\widetilde O(n^7/f)$ copies and polynomial classical processing. Connected quartic correlations reveal the hidden mode groups, and fresh local measurements restore the branches and their coherences. No particle-number conservation, minimum branch weight or spectral gap is assumed.

papers.title: On the coincidence of discrete and continuous definitions of Entanglement of Formation
papers.summary: It is proved that every Borel ensemble of pure states on a separable bipartite Hilbert space with finite average entanglement admits a countable ensemble with the same barycenter and arbitrarily small additional average entanglement. Consequently, the discrete and continuous versions of the Entanglement of Formation coincide on the whole space of states of infinite-dimensional bipartite quantum system (with infinite values allowed). The main idea of the proof (realized with the AI-assistance) is the lifting a Borel ensemble of pure bipartite states to a Borel probability measure on the unit sphere in the space of Hilbert--Schmidt operators followed by dividing the support of this measure into appropriate cells and replacing each cell by its conditional barycenter. The resulting countable ensemble is obtained by a recursive construction.

papers.title: A modular quantum computer based on Cornucopia codes
papers.summary: Ultra-high-rate quantum error correction codes store many logical qubits in a single code block with few physical qubits. A fault-tolerant quantum computer, however, also requires a universal set of logical operations on individually addressable logical qubits, and the ancilla overhead of these operations may erode the advantage of the high encoding rate. Here, we propose the Cornucopia architecture, in which a universal set of logical operations is implemented at low overhead for the Cornucopia codes. In particular, we focus on the [[2844,1426,18]] Cornucopia code as an example and introduce a modular quantum computer built from such code blocks connected by bridges. Each block stores 1,426 logical qubits and serves as a universal logical processor. Exploiting the code's translation symmetry, we construct a family of reusable gadgets that individually address 1,422 logical qubits within each block. These gadgets support three universal logical instruction sets: basic, high-throughput and fixed-extractor. Excluding magic-state factories, a module with sufficient workspace to execute any instruction in the basic set requires an average of 4.1 physical qubits per logical qubit, compared with 3.0 for memory alone. The architecture thus preserves the resource advantage of ultra-high-rate quantum memory while enabling universal logical computation, providing a route towards low-overhead fault-tolerant quantum computers.

papers.title: Exact analytical spectra of an effective field-modified radial Schr\"odinger equation by the Nikiforov--Uvarov method
papers.summary: We revisit the effective radial Schr\"odinger equation for a charged spinless particle in collinear static electric and magnetic fields that was formulated in our earlier work within the tridiagonal representation approach (TRA). In that model the angular factor of the electric coupling is replaced by the orientation parameter $C=\cos\theta$, the linear Zeeman term is diagonal in the azimuthal quantum number, and the effective field-modified central potential takes the form $V(r)=\Vt(r)+qECr$. Here we show that the same equation can be solved exactly without the TRA, by the Nikiforov--Uvarov (NU) method, once the potential component $\Vt(r)$ is prescribed. Three examples are worked out in closed form: a Kratzer-type component, which yields a linear-plus-Coulomb-plus-inverse-square central potential; a pseudoharmonic-type component, which yields a linear-plus-harmonic-plus-inverse-square potential; and a Hulth\'en-type component with a repulsive core (Manning--Rosen form), which yields a screened confining potential with a finite number of $s$-wave bound states. For each case we obtain the energy spectrum, the normalized eigenfunctions in terms of Laguerre or Jacobi polynomials, the location of the potential minimum, and closed-form radial moments. The spectra are independent of the orientation $\theta$ and of the electric field, in agreement with the structure found by the TRA, while the field enters through the shape of $V(r)$, the radial moments, and the expectation value $\langle V\rangle_k$. All analytical results are confirmed by an independent finite-difference diagonalization.

papers.title: Quantum Superposition Principle and Geometry
papers.summary: If one takes seriously the postulate of quantum mechanics in which physical states are rays in the standard Hilbert space of the theory, one is naturally lead to a geometric formulation of the theory. Within this formulation of quantum mechanics, the resulting description is very elegant from the geometrical viewpoint, since it allows to cast the main postulates of the theory in terms of two geometric structures, namely a symplectic structure and a Riemannian metric. However, the usual superposition principle of quantum mechanics is not naturally incorporated, since the quantum state space is non-linear. In this note we offer some steps to incorporate the superposition principle within the geometric description. In this respect, we argue that it is necessary to make the distinction between a 'projective superposition principle' and a 'decomposition principle' that extend the standard superposition principle. We illustrate our proposal with two very well known examples, namely the spin 1/2 system and the two slit experiment, where the distinction is clear from the physical perspective. We show that the two principles have also a different mathematical origin within the geometrical formulation of the theory.

papers.title: The Dry Ten Martini Problem at Criticality
papers.summary: We solve the dry ten martini problem (lean-verified this time) by showing that every labeled almost Mathieu gap is open for $\lambda\neq 0$ and every irrational frequency. In particular, we prove that the maximum logarithmic height of each labeled gap is non-decreasing in the coupling $\lambda$ and extend an initial open seed gap for each gap label $n$ from $\lambda\in(0,\lambda_{n})$ to all $\lambda> 0$. The non-decreasing property follows from restoring time-reversal symmetry to the almost Mathieu operator $H$ by pairing it with its magnetic inverse $\bar{H}$. This allows us to express the logarithmic coupling derivative of the maximal gap height as the expectation value of a non-negative operator, yielding the required monotonicity.

papers.title: Dark Subspaces and Invariant Measures of Quantum Trajectories
papers.summary: Quantum trajectories are Markov processes describing the evolution of a quantum system subject to indirect measurements. They can be viewed as place dependent iterated function systems or the result of products of dependent and non identically distributed random matrices. In this article, we establish a complete classification of their invariant measures. The classification is done in two steps. First, we prove a Markov process on some linear subspaces called dark subspaces, defined in (Maassen, K\"ummerer 2006), admits a unique invariant measure. Second, we study the process inside the dark subspaces. Using a notion of minimal family of isometries from a reference space to dark subspaces, we prove a set of measures indexed by orbits of a unitary group is the set of ergodic measures of quantum trajectories.

papers.title: Fluctuation-Induced Supersolidity at the Superfluid-Solid Interface
papers.summary: Supersolidity, combining superfluid and crystalline orders, has been realized in dipolar Bose-Einstein condensates by tuning interatomic interactions. Here we show that supersolidity can also emerge from mode coupling at a superfluid-solid interface, without modifying bulk interactions and for a broad class of superfluids. Using an analytical and numerical treatment of the coupled superfluid and phonon fields, we derive the criterion for a density-modulation instability driven by interfacial coupling and dependent on dimensionality. In superfluid helium, the instability first appears at the roton mode, while in a Bose-Einstein condensate with contact interactions it occurs at the lowest accessible wave vector set by the system size. Beyond the threshold, the ground state acquires an interfacial density modulation while the bulk remains superfluid, forming a hybrid superfluid-supersolid phase. Our results identify interfacial mode coupling as a promising route to supersolidity, enabling the simultaneous exploitation of interfacial supersolid and bulk superfluid quantum properties.

papers.title: Why finite-size non-Hermitian eigenvalues can miss asymptotic eigenstates in topological physics
papers.summary: Non-Hermitian systems exhibit a fundamental spectral dichotomy absent in Hermitian physics: the eigenvalue spectrum and the eigenstate spectrum can deviate significantly in the thermodynamic limit. We explain how extrapolating finite-size eigenvalues can miss important asymptotic eigenstates, with the unidirectional Hatano-Nelson model serving as a minimal realization of this phenomenon. Through exact analytical solutions, we show that this model contains not only hidden asymptotic modes but also quasi-Jordan structures that become macroscopic in the thermodynamic limit and appear more generally in systems with nontrivial bulk winding. Our framework explains how the apparent failure of the bulk-edge correspondence in models such as the non-Hermitian SSH chain can reflect the failure of finite-size eigenvalue extrapolation to detect asymptotic edge states in systems with a skin effect. These results clarify the limitations of using finite-size eigenvalues alone to infer thermodynamic-limit topology.

papers.title: Emergent chiral Higgs mode in $\pi$-flux frustrated lattices
papers.summary: Neutral-atom quantum simulators provide a powerful platform for realizing strongly correlated phases, enabling access to dynamical signatures of quasiparticles and symmetry breaking processes. Motivated by recent observations of quantum phases in flux-frustrated ladders with non-vanishing ground state currents, we investigate interacting bosons on the dimerized BBH lattice in two dimensions-originally introduced in the context of higher-order topology. After mapping out the phase diagram, which includes vortex superfluid (V-SF), vortex Mott insulator (V-MI), and featureless Mott insulator (MI) phases, we focus on the integer filling case. There, the MI/V-SF transition simultaneously breaks the $\mathbb Z_2^{T}$ and U(1) symmetries, where $\mathbb Z_2^{T}$ corresponds to time-reversal symmetry (TRS). Using a slave-boson description, we resolve the excitation spectrum across the transition and uncover a chiral Higgs mode whose mass softens at criticality, providing a dynamical hallmark of emergent chirality that manifests via the oscillation of the loop currents in quench dynamics. Our results establish an experimentally realistic setting for probing unconventional TRS-broken phases and quasiparticles with intrinsic chirality in strongly interacting quantum matter.
